en: Compiled by Shi Dunlun, Volume 4, Section on Yoga (Part 8a), Main Treatise, Scroll 33.
Within the Fourth Section on Yoga, there are initially two verses that enumerate two gateways; subsequently, based upon...
The analysis by way of gates. Regarding the two gates:
the first is the gate of entering the world.
The second concerns the supramundane.
"Mundane" refers to the tainted virtues such as the subduing of afflictions, the attainment of meditative concentration, and the cultivation of the five mundane supernormal powers.
"Supramundane" refers to the untainted virtues from the sixteen noble practices up to the attainment of the fruits [of the path].
Now, it is explained that the cultivation of these two merits constitutes the essence of the fourth yoga.
Master Jing’s judgment states:
The preceding verse enumerates mundane yoga,
while the subsequent verse enumerates supramundane yoga.
Regarding the first yoga, there are six sections.
First, clarifying the seven types of mental attention for subduing afflictions;
second, extensively distinguishing the eight meditative absorptions;
third, clarifying the attainment of non-conception and the attainment of cessation.

Fourth, the discrimination of the four analytical knowledges and the five supernormal powers. Fifth, the distinction between the reduction of births and the meritorious qualities associated with outflows.
Sixth, the characteristics of those who have abandoned desire.
Regarding the subsequent verse on supramundane practice, it states:

"One observes the truths. This refers to the fact that even prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one still gives rise to the mental attention of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣamanasikāra*) characterized by signs (*sanimitta*).
The mental application of discerning characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*) consists of the five cessations and the general and specific applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
The mental application of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣika manaskāra*) consists of the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), wherein one contemplates the four truths.
As for "thoroughly penetrating according to reality," it refers to the following:

That is to say, during the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one cultivates the mental application of detachment (*viveka-manasikāra*) to penetrate the suchness (*tathatā*) of the four truths and permanently sever the afflictions of seeing (*darśana-heya-kleśa*).

Regarding the detailed classification of those who cultivate [the path], this involves the mental application of observation (*mīmāṃsā-manasikāra*), which observes whether the afflictions of both seeing and cultivation have been severed or remain; furthermore, it involves the mental application of joy in grasping (*ratisaṃgrāhaka-manasikāra*), which proceeds to sever the afflictions of cultivation, attaining the second and third fruits of the path of cultivation, and continuing until the eighth grade of the afflictions of cultivation below the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) has been severed.

Furthermore, the "attention of the culmination of application" (*prayoganiṣṭha-manasikāra*) that arises again is the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), which is the ninth path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
it is the ultimate state for those who follow.
This is precisely the fruit of the culmination of application (*prayoga-niṣṭhā-phala*).

Its stage is that of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), consisting of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). Jī provides the following commentary:
The first verse clarifies that there are seven [topics] in one section;
the second line clarifies the seven types of mental attention (*manasikāra*) within the initial inquiry.
First, the seven gateways are explained:
First, the cultivation of mental attention;
second, the abandonment of desire;
third, the detailed exposition of the various meditative concentrations.
4. The two meditative absorptions;
5. the five supernormal powers;
6. the distinction of the primary [subject].
The seven characteristics emerge from the fourth [stage], taking this as their essence.
While the first three were explained in the context of the second and third stages, and the fourth was clarified in the section on the purification of obstacles, we now explain the fifth:
the cultivation of mental attention (*manasikāra*).
This is the major section of the thirtieth [chapter].
Now, following the previous classification,
we shall distinguish the Middle Way according to its gates.
First, a brief explanation of the two gates;
second, a detailed analysis beginning with the question, "How many kinds are there herein?
Regarding the former, those practitioners of yoga who have already attained mental attention (*manasikāra*) and have entered such a state of partial joy and abandonment:
This concludes the preceding explanation of the seven mental attentions (manasikāra) included within the stage of meditative concentration (samāhitabhūmi),
which have been attained by a beginner practitioner who delights in abandoning the afflictions (kleśa) and delights in realizing nirvāṇa.
From this point forward, for the practitioner who has first begun their training, there are only two destinies.
Within the extensive explanation, the main text is divided into two parts.
First, up to the end of this fascicle, the destinies that lead to the supramundane are explained.
In the latter part of this fascicle, the transcendence of the mundane world is elucidated.
Within the former part, first, six gates are briefly distinguished;
second, these six gates are extensively distinguished.
Briefly, there are four types of individuals who initiate the application of effort to transcend the world.
Regarding the fourth type of person, this refers to all bodhisattvas who delight in attaining great enlightenment in a future life rather than in the present existence.
Master Ji said:
"This meaning clarifies that the fruit of Buddhahood for a bodhisattva in the future is not a phenomenon of the present.
Although the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) of the worldly path belong to the present life,"
However, because they accomplish the maturation of sentient beings within birth and death through application to the mundane path,
if a woman’s mind is directed toward the fruit of Buddhahood, she then initiates application to the supramundane path.
Now, according to the previous meaning, there are again two types:
first, those with full fetters, which refers to all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); second, those with incomplete fetters, which refers to all those in training (*śaikṣa*).
Question: How is it that those in training initiate application (*prayoga*) for the sake of taking birth in the world?
The commentary explains:
Among the four [stages], from the second and fourth productions of the thought of enlightenment onward, they are all termed "those in training" (śaikṣa).
Because they have partially subdued and cultivated the afflictions of the bhāvanā-mārga, they are termed "not fully bound" (asambaddha).
This refers to first contemplating the desire realm as being of a coarse nature and so forth;
this is a brief exposition of the seven mental attentions (*manasikāra*) for the abandonment of desire and the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*).
Furthermore, based on the dhyānas and so forth, the latter four gates are briefly explained below.
Tài said: "There are four types of people who subdue their afflictions through six practices.
The first are the various non-Buddhists."
Second, within the internal dharmas, those who have long cultivated the practice of meditative concentration suppress all manifest entanglements solely by means of the six modes of conduct.

Third, although their innate faculties are sharp, because they do not apply themselves to the stages of "warmth" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, they are unable to give rise to the contemplation of the truths; thus, having fallen back from the state of detachment, they must again employ the six modes of conduct to suppress afflictions, give rise to meditative concentration, or be reborn in a higher realm.

Because the four great bodhisattvas have not yet exhausted their residual afflictions (*kleśa-avaśeṣa*), they give rise to the six modes of practice to suppress these afflictions and manifest supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
Furthermore, it is said that those in training (*śaikṣa*) have already severed the afflictions of the four stages, beginning with the desire realm.

Because one can give rise to the meditative attainment of cessation by suppressing the afflictions of the five stages through the mundane path, and because the non-returner also gives rise to the sixfold practice;

this author of the treatise cites the mindless attainments in response to the previous question: "How is it that those in training who have attained the first two fruits cannot suppress the afflictions and obtain the fundamental dhyānas?"
If one were to attain the fundamental dhyāna, one would necessarily attain the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*);
yet, although this interpretation has been offered, it does not accord with the literal sense of the text.

For although this section explains the practices of the śrāvakas, it concludes by summarizing those who dwell in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*) and initiate application in the mundane realm.
Therefore, to clarify the Great Bodhisattva,
the following second section provides an extensive analysis in six gates, beginning with "having already become free from the desires of the desire realm."
This consists of six sections.
The first explains detachment through the seven types of mental attention (*manasikāra*).
It first clarifies how the seven kinds of mental attention bring about detachment from the desires of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Second, the explanation of the seven types of mental attention (*manasikāra*) that abandon desire for the stages from above the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Within this, first there is a general enumeration,
followed by a detailed explanation.
Within this, there are four sections:
first, the sequential and individual explanation of the seven mental attentions (*manasikāra*);
second, the clarification that when these mental attentions proceed, joy and bliss gradually increase until they reach a state of fullness, which constitutes the fruit of cultivation as an antidote.
The threefold explanation clarifies the distinctions in the functions of mental attention (*manasikāra*).
Fourthly, it explains how these are subsumed under the four types of mental attention.
Within the first section, the first part explains the mental attention that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manasikāra*).
This refers to being able to discern the coarse characteristics (*audārikatva*) of the desire realm and the tranquil characteristics (*śāntatva*) of the first dhyāna.
Master Ji states that within the Hīnayāna, all six aspects of the practice must be performed.
Now, in the Mahāyāna, one attains [enlightenment] through a single practice alone;
it is not necessary to possess all six practices.
Among these six practices, one may cultivate whichever one corresponds to one's mental attention.
Regarding the statement that "the basis for pleasant feeling is the locus of craving,
and it is the locus of the inversion of perception and the inversion of mind," Master Jing and others say:
In the Mahāyāna, based on the meaning of greed (*rāga*), there are explained the inversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*) and the inversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*).
Therefore, the objective basis of greed is precisely the inversion of perception,
which is also the objective basis for the inversion of mind.
Regarding the statement that "the basis for feeling neither-pain-nor-pleasure is the basis for delusion, and so forth, up to being the basis for the inversion of views":
because views arise from delusion,
the basis for delusion is itself the basis for the inversion of views.
Among these, that which takes [objects] as its cognitive object is called the desire for afflictions;
that which is the object itself is called the desire for things.
This applies within the common characteristics of vitarka and vicāra.

Regarding the statement that "all desires" refers to the suffering of birth and so forth up to the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, but does not mention the eighth type, the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*),
Ji says: "This is stated here according to what is commonly known in the world."
The suffering commonly known in the world is spoken of without reference to ultimate suffering.
Although this ultimate suffering exists in all desires and all things,
it is not mentioned because it is difficult to perceive.
Now, having set aside the general [category] and proceeding to the specific,
it is omitted and not mentioned.
One investigates the coarse aspects among all desires.
The statement, "It is like a chain of bones, even unto a fruit at the tip of a tree," clarifies the faults by means of these eight similes.
Tai Ji and others say:
In this regard, it is as loathsome as a skeleton;
it is like congealed blood and flesh— without blood, congealed into flesh, unreal, and loathsome.
Like a grass torch that is extinguished in an instant,
or like a single ember of charcoal capable of burning a mountain or marsh, so too can even a small portion of sensual desires destroy a vast multitude of roots of goodness.
The rest is as previously described.
Furthermore, it is explained that when the body touches fire, it results in a grave illness;
yet, by not touching it, one returns to a state of moderate well-being and attains pleasure.
Desire is just like this.
Furthermore, it is said that just as a portion of charcoal may have fire while another portion lacks fire, [desire] is something to be loathed.
This interpretation is incorrect when one investigates the coarse principle of desire.
The judgment that [the food] arises from great provisions and great seeking constitutes the principle of dependency (*apekṣā-yukti*).
The subsequent explanation that food can counteract the suffering of hunger and thirst illustrates the principle of efficacy (*kāritra-yukti*).

Furthermore, those various desires are established by the authority of the scriptures (*āptāgama*), direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and the principles of logical proof (*upapatti-sādhana*).
Moreover, from beginningless time, those various desires are established by the principle of the nature of things (*dharmatā-yukti*).
Now, the second principle of functional efficacy (*kāryakāraṇayukti*) is judged as follows:
it is the passage beginning with "Furthermore, although those various desires arise well and increase well," and ending with "even for the sake of curing a disease, one takes foul medicine."
The rest is as previously determined.
T’ai says: Within the sense bases of the desire realm, there is the physical body with its material faculties, which is characterized by heaviness (dausthulya).
Unlike those in the Form Realm, who are subtle and light,
[beings here] are nourished by solid food and clothed in garments.
Or they may be destroyed and severed by others;
or again, death occurs as a natural dissolution and extinction inherent to all phenomena;
or else, one must constantly counteract the various kinds of suffering that arise within oneself.
Regarding the explanation of the mental application of seclusion (*viveka-manasikāra*),
Master Sthiramati comments on the phrase: "that which first gives rise to the path for abandoning the afflictions."
The two types of attention (*manasikāra*) are not said to sever the afflictions;
it is the third, "separation," that can sever the afflictions;
therefore, it is said that the path of initial abandonment arises.
Question: Just as the two ends of a scale rise and fall simultaneously,
why is it that when the mind of the form realm (rūpadhātu) attains its characteristic of clarity, the afflictions (kleśa) of the desire realm (kāmadhātu) have not yet been eliminated?
The commentary states:

Prior to the "understanding of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī*), although one may cultivate weariness toward desire through hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī*) within the desire realm, this is not yet able to accord with the abandonment of the afflictions of the lower realms.
This superior resolution (*adhimokṣa*) of understanding the characteristics, however, can accord with seclusion and abandon the desires of the lower realms.
Therefore, although the resolution that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedin-adhimokṣa*) does not sever the afflictions (*kleśa*), the afflictions do not arise;
this is just as when a person who has attained the first fruit (*prathamaphala*) attains the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*) while still not yet free from desire through cultivation.
At present, the discernment of characteristics is likewise so.
Even without having abandoned the lower-grade afflictions and so forth, one immediately attains the "characteristic of comprehension.
Although the afflictions do not arise when this characteristic of comprehension arises—
just as an unwholesome mind does not arise when a wholesome mind arises— [the afflictions remain].
It does not arise because it has not been abandoned; it does not arise because the mental attention (*manasikāra*) that brings about abandonment has been distanced.
In the first two stages, the first two types of mental attention have still not been abandoned.
If there is an intermittent arising of desire and evil,
it is resolved within the latter two types of mental attention (*manasikāra*).
Furthermore, Ki explains:
Regarding the explanation of the *manaskāra* of the culmination of preparation (*prayoganiṣṭha-manaskāra*), it states:
"By reason of these causes and conditions, from that which is bound to the desire realm up to what is called the *manaskāra* of the culmination of preparation.
Herein, the explanation of the six practices for subduing afflictions indicates that one does not attain the realization of the subsequent path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Therefore, it is said that they are "temporarily suppressed and severed.
Regarding this suppression and severance, both the suppression of the active manifestations (*paryavasthāna*) and the suppression of the seeds (*bīja*) must be achieved. How is this known?
The commentary on the first two types of attention states:
"In the second type of attention, although afflictions do not arise because it is not interrupted by hearing or reflection,
it is not yet called the 'uninterrupted path' (ānantarya-mārga) because the active defilements have not been suppressed."

In the third stage of mental attention (*manasikāra*), when the capacity for the seeds to produce manifest results is suppressed, it is only then designated as the "uninterrupted path" (*ānantarya-mārga*).
For these contaminated practices (*sāsrava-carita*), this is how it functions;
however, for uncontaminated practices (*anāsrava-carita*), they are only designated as the uninterrupted path once the seeds have been severed.
Although the manifest [afflictions] do not arise, it still constitutes the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*);
the present case is likewise.
Subduing the manifest [afflictions] serves as the path of preparation, while subduing the seeds serves as the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Regarding the statement, "Immediately following this seventh mental application (*manasikāra*),

by means of these causes and conditions, one realizes entry into the fundamental first dhyāna," the intended meaning of the treatise here is that the ninth path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) abides in the fundamental dhyāna.
The nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) all occur within the preparatory concentrations (*sāmantaka*).
Regarding this, there are two interpretations.

The first interpretation holds that, from the first dhyāna up to the third dhyāna, the nine paths of uninterrupted transition and the [first] nine paths of liberation occur in the preparatory stages, while the ninth path of liberation occurs either in the preparatory stage or in the fundamental concentration (*maula-samādhi*).

If one is in the ninth path of liberation of the fourth dhyāna or above, the concentration is necessarily in the fundamental absorption (mauladhyāna); however, the first eight paths of liberation and the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (anantaryamārga) are in the preparatory stage (sāmantaka). Why is this so?
In the three dhyānas and below, because joy and bliss exist in the fundamental stages, while equanimity exists in the preparatory stages;

in the fundamental stages, whether during meditative observation or the abandonment of afflictions, there is no feeling of equanimity, as it is absent due to the nature of those states being characterized by darkness. It is definitively non-existent.
Because they possess joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), clarity (*āloka*), and sharpness (*paṭutva*), they exist.

Within their preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), whether it be the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśaprahāṇa*) or meditative observation (*anupaśyanā*), there is always equanimity (*upekṣā*) and clarity; however, joy and bliss exist only during meditative observation, for joy and bliss do not occur at the time of abandoning afflictions.

In the three dhyānas and below, there are two types of persons—those of sharp and dull faculties—who give rise to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
If a person of sharp faculties is on the ninth path of uninterrupted transition, they abide in the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*).
The ninth path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) abides in the fundamental dhyāna and is associated with joy and bliss (*prīti-sukha*).

If the person is of dull faculties (*mṛdu-indriya*), the ninth path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) abides in the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) and is associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Because his mind is dull, he is unable to enter the fundamental dhyāna quickly to be associated with joy and bliss;
thus, his ninth path of liberation abides in the preparatory stage (sāmantaka) and is associated with equanimity.
Regarding the statement that the seventh mental application (*manasikāra*) enters the fundamental absorption (*mauladhyāna*):
this refers to those of sharp faculties who are able to enter the fundamental absorption swiftly, which is associated with bliss and so forth.
This seventh mental application takes up the three dhyānas.
If one abides in the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*), the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) is associated with equanimity (*upekṣāvedanā*).
If there is a fundamental dhyāna (*mauladhyāna*), the path of liberation is associated with pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth.
Regarding the four dhyānas above that, the first eight liberations and nine uninterrupted paths all reside within the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*);
however, the ninth liberation must necessarily reside in the fundamental concentration (*mauladhyāna*) and does not abide in the preparatory stage.
This is the ultimate truth.
Furthermore, it is said:
"If one does not analyze in this way, the nine uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*) would reside within the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*)."
The ninth path of liberation resides within the fundamental meditative absorptions;
this applies from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
What evidence is there for this preceding point?

If one explains the stages in general without distinguishing that the first six modes of attention (*manasikāra*) belong to the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) while the seventh belongs to the fundamental stage (*maula*),
but merely states that they constitute the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), this serves as a proof for our position.
I have not yet seen a textual passage that takes "discrimination" as its essential point;
therefore, the latter meaning uses this very text as proof.
The interpretation of this text in the preceding section is consistent with the previous explanation regarding those of dull and sharp faculties.
This will be explained in detail later in the section on the "empty state.

Furthermore, following the passage on the manifestation of the attention that consists of the enjoyment of seclusion (*viveka-kāma-manasikāra*), the second [section] clarifies the fruit of the antidote: dwelling filled with joy and bliss while the four types of attention are manifesting.
Question: Among the seven modes of attention (*manasikāra*), why are only these four explained as possessing a sense of gratification? Answer:
It is explained as follows:

The three mental orientations (*manasikāra*)—detachment (*viveka*), enjoyment (*rati*), and the culmination of application (*prayoga-niṣṭha*)—bring about an increase in well-being because they directly eliminate the heavy residues (*dausthulya*) through the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).

Although the mental orientation that is the fruit of the culmination of application (*prayoga-niṣṭhā-phala*) is not the path of immediate succession that directly severs the afflictions (*kleśa*), [it still contributes to well-being].
However, this liberation is preeminent because it is initially free from desire and ultimately possesses a great increase of joy;
therefore, it is specifically mentioned among the other three types of attention.
The first two are the path of preparation;
the attention of observation is the path of excellence,
which differs from the preceding four.
Therefore, it is not discussed [here]. Furthermore, regarding the mental application that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*), below [the section on] what is to be abandoned,
the third section provides a detailed explanation of the distinctions in the functions of mental application.
The *manaskāra* of "comprehending characteristics" involves understanding that sensual desires are evil and should be abandoned, and that meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) should be attained.
The *manaskāra* of "investigation" involves knowing the limits of what is known and remaining free from overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
The remaining five are as stated in the text.
Tai says: "The Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) universally agrees that in the preparatory concentration (anāgamya-samādhi), there are no feelings of joy or bliss;
yet now, this treatise alone distinguishes these feelings of joy and bliss."
Having abandoned the attachment to pleasure and severed the first two categories [of afflictions], one abides in the preliminary concentration (anāgamya-dhyāna) accompanied by joy and bliss;
however, because one occasionally gives rise to equanimity (*upekṣā*) in response to what is asked,
the joy and bliss accompanying the culmination of the application (*prayoga-niṣṭha*) do not pervade the entire body, and equanimity also arises intermittently.
Because joy and bliss arise in constant succession at the time of fruition, it is not said that they occur "from time to time.
Jì (基) says: "As stated in the twenty-eighth [fascicle]: [and so forth].
The former two are both paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).
As for the present case, where only resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) constitutes the primary path of preparation,
this is stated with reference to a superior stage, a stage proximate to the immediate path (*ānantarya-mārga*), and a stage not interrupted by hearing or reflection (*śruta-cintā*).
Therefore, it is said that only resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) constitutes the correct preparatory application (*prayoga*).
The preceding twenty-eight [factors] are discussed in terms of their actual reality;
the clear discernment of characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī*) is likewise a preparatory application.

Another interpretation is that this "correctly initiating the preparatory application" (*prayoga*) does not necessarily exclude the path of discerning characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisamvedana*), which is not itself a preparatory path;
for it is superior due to its proximity to the stage of "resolute conviction" (*adhimokṣa*).
This explains that the correct application of effort (*prayoga*) is indeed initiated;
furthermore, while it speaks of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) as the correct application, this does not exclude the characteristic of thorough comprehension (*parijñā-lakṣaṇa*).
In reality, there is no contradiction.
Furthermore, for what reason is it that after describing the abandonment of the superior grade,
one does not say "free from overweening pride," nor does one say "free from overweening pride" after the third grade of abandonment,
but rather says "free from overweening pride" after the abandonment of the middling and inferior grades?
The commentary states:
The delusions of the first six categories are coarse and easy to recognize;
the delusions of the final three categories are subtle and difficult to discern.
Having abandoned the superior, medium, and lower grades of the preceding defilements, one mistakenly believes that the lowest grade of defilements no longer exists;

thus, giving rise to overweening pride (*abhimāna*), one claims that all nine grades have been exhausted and that one has already cultivated and realized the fundamental meditative absorption (*mauladhyāna*).

Now, having abandoned this pride, one speaks of being free from overweening pride (*adhimāna*) after the abandonment of medium-grade afflictions; it is not said that one is free from it after [abandoning] superior-grade [afflictions].
Furthermore, regarding the "attention consisting of the discernment of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*) and below:
Regarding the fourth point, concerning the inclusion of the six types of mental attention within the four types of mental attention and the two remedies of weariness and abandonment,
Master Ki’s explanation is as follows:
"The meaning here is that these [six] are included within thirty types of mental attention and are subsumed under the four remedies."
The forty modes of attention (*manasikāra*) are explained as before in the eleventh fascicle.

It is now stated that the "attention that discerns characteristics" (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manasikāra*) and the "attention of resolute conviction" (*adhimokṣika manasikāra*) are collectively termed "conformable attention" (*anulomika manasikāra*), as they both function in conjunction with the antidote of repudiation (*vidūṣaṇā-pratipakṣa*).
Among the forty types of attention, the attention of conformity (*ānulomika-manasikāra*) constitutes twenty-five;
for the attention of conformity brings about the revulsion toward the object of focus, thereby conducing to the abandonment of the afflictions.

The first two types of attention are "conformable" because they are in accordance [with the goal]; furthermore, the attention of withdrawal and the attention of the culmination of application are called "counteractive" attention, as they function together with the counteractive abandonment.
The application of attention as an antidote is the twenty-sixth.
Regarding the application of attention as an antidote:
it refers to that by means of which one correctly abandons all afflictions.
Because these two constitute the paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*),
they are subsumed under the attention of counteraction (*pratipakṣa-manasikāra*).

Furthermore, the attention of "delight in cultivation" (*ratisaṃgrāhaka-manasikāra*) is designated as both the attention of counteraction and the attention conducive to purification (*viśuddhy-anukūla-manasikāra*).
Regarding the mental application conducive to purification,
it consists of twenty-seven types.
Regarding the mental application conducive to purification:
This refers to the cultivation of the six recollections, namely the recollection of the Buddha and so forth.
Because the mental attention that embraces joy (*ratisaṃgrāhaka-manasikāra*) abandons the medium-grade afflictions, it is called "antidotal mental attention" (*pratipakṣika-manasikāra*).
Since one clearly takes the six recollections as objects and cultivates a distinct contemplation of the purity of nirvāṇa, the Buddha, and so forth, these are also termed "pure."
Because it has a distinct object, it is explained separately from the "exclusive" (*asādhāraṇa*) and other [mental applications] in a single location.

Furthermore, since the preceding [categories], such as "separation" (*viveka*), do not include the mental application that accords with purification (*viśuddhi-anulomika-manaskāra*), this [category] includes it accordingly.
Question: Why are the four counteractive measures (pratipakṣa) not included herein? Answer:
[The reason is as follows:]
Because it is manifested by its shadow.
It should be understood that this teaching on the abandonment of afflictions refers exclusively to "separation" as the antidote.
If that is so, why does it not mention "concomitance"?
The commentary states:
"Counteractive measures (pratipakṣa) are wisdom (prajñā), while mental attention (manasikāra) is the mind (manas).
The preceding text further includes counteractive measures [within the category of wisdom]."
When the mind and wisdom proceed together, it is called "concomitant.
In this context, only attention (manasikāra) is clarified, not the antidote;
because wisdom is absent, "concomitant" is not mentioned.

Furthermore, if one observes that the mental engagement of investigation is called "mental engagement in accordance with investigation," it should consist of twenty-eight types of mental engagement in accordance with investigation.
This refers to observing whether the various afflictions have been abandoned or not, and observing the principles of the dharmas previously realized;
this, in relation to what preceded it, is also the antidote of distant separation and so forth.
I shall not elaborate further here.
In relation to the preceding stage of "separation," this is called the "antidote of distancing" (*dūrabhāga-pratipakṣa*) because it is the path of progress (*pratipad*).
In relation to the "attention of delight in grasping" (*ratisaṃgrāhaka-manaskāra*), this is the "antidote of maintenance" (*ādhāra-pratipakṣa*) because it is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Now, because these are explained following the "conforming to delight" (*anurāga*), their inclusion within the "counteracting characteristics" (*pratipakṣa-lakṣaṇa*) is not mentioned;
for they were already shown to be mutually exclusive previously.
Furthermore, it says:

Regarding the statement, "In this way, it should be known that the remaining four types of attention are subsumed within the six types of attention, namely, the attention of conformity (*ānulomika-manasikāra*) and so forth," the meaning is as follows:
these four types of attention are termed "remaining" because they are external to the [first] seven types of attention.
These four modes of attention (*manasikāra*) are among the forty modes of attention;
since they are now subsumed within six of the seven modes of attention,
it is said that they are "included within the six modes of attention."
Question: Why are the characteristics of the seventh mental application (*manasikāra*), such as its inclusion [within other categories], not explained here? Answer:
The seventh mental application (*manasikāra*) is the fruit;
these four mental applications, together with the preceding six, are all causes.
Causes may be mutually inclusive, but fruits cannot.
Therefore, the seventh mental application (*manasikāra*) is not included.
Since the forty [applications] are subsumed within these seven here,
it is only these four that are subsumed.
In the text of that eleventh section, forty [mental applications] are used to subsume the seven;
that is, within those seven, the meaning is fully encompassed by forty mental applications.
Now, however, it is the seven that subsume the forty, not the forty that subsume the seven.
Therefore, there are differences regarding non-exhaustion and non-collection; examine this.
Second, from here on, it clarifies the seven types of mental attention that abandon desire for the stages above the first dhyāna, up to the sphere of nothingness.
This section is divided into three parts:
first, it introduces the general category of the initial concentration, stating that all higher stages possess seven types of attention;
second, it addresses those stages from "with vitarka and vicāra" downwards.
Separately, based on the higher [realms] and departing from the lower, there are seven mental orientations (*manaskāra*).
Thirdly, regarding "the coarse characteristics of those [lower realms]," this explains the investigation of the two kinds of coarse characteristics through six matters.
Regarding the detailed explanation,
there are two interpretations of the phrase "already entered and already attained.
One interpretation states that because one is physically in the desire realm while entering the first dhyāna, it is called "already entered."
It is called "already attained" because one is born in that stage;
it is called "realized entry" because one is currently in meditative absorption.
Although one does not enter [the state] while already having attained it, it is therefore called "already attained."
Regarding the statement, "If it is in a state of meditative concentration (*samāhita-bhūmi*),
it is called *vicāra*," Jing says:
Since these modes of *vitarka* and *vicāra* possess coarseness and subtlety respectively, they cannot arise simultaneously.
Among the eightfold noble path, right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) is vitarka.
Vitarka has volition (*cetanā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) as its intrinsic nature.
Right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*) is also wisdom.
Within a single moment of thought, there are not two wisdoms existing simultaneously;
yet, for the sake of conventional explanation, they may be described as two.
Furthermore, right contemplation (samyak-saṃkalpa) has volition (cetanā) as its intrinsic nature.
Right view has wisdom as its intrinsic nature;
they arise simultaneously as distinct entities. Tai says:
Names and phrases are able to express phenomena;
the mental faculty is able to discern phenomena;
and the coarse mental faculty, together with vitarka, is also able to discern phenomena.
Because the discernment of the meaning of dharmas resembles names and phrases, it is called "mental discourse" (manojalpa).
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that "discourse" (jalpa) refers to mental reflection, not to vocal speech.
It is called "mental discourse" (manojalpa) because it proceeds together with intention, volition, nature, and verbal designation.
Ji states: "Name" refers to the phenomena that express themselves through words.
Its substance is coarse.
Because mental investigation (*manas-vitarka*) is able to contemplate all phenomena as resembling names and phrases,
it is said to have the nature of mental verbalization (*manojalpa*).
Furthermore, "speech" is the name for verbal expression;
"reflection" is the name for mental activity.
Since vitarka is the name for reflection, [it follows that]...
Therefore, it is called "mental verbalization" (*manojalpa*).
In the Hīnayāna, vitarka and vicāra are associated with the fundamental [dhyāna]. Some say:
Now, it is not so in the Mahāyāna.
To claim that investigation and analysis (vitarka-vicāra) exist only during the stage of skillful means (upāya) is incorrect.
Another passage further states: "In meditative concentration, there is no vitarka or vicāra;
there is no vitarka or vicāra that initiates speech, but it is not that subtle vitarka and vicāra are absent."
Furthermore, it is because the five factors are not established as factors of the fundamental dhyānas.

Moreover, regarding the statement that "one correctly understands that such vitarka and vicāra are of the nature of mental factors (*cittadharma*) and so forth," this merely explains that vitarka and vicāra are of the nature of mental concomitants (*caitta*) and arise simultaneously with the mind.
Not understanding that vitarka and vicāra are naturally associated with themselves,
[one might think] that what arises depending on the internal is included within the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*).
[However,] that which arises depending on the internal faculties has as its substance the dharma-object (*dharmaviṣaya*).
They are subsumed under the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*).

Furthermore, one correctly understands that such discursive thoughts and investigations (*vitarka-vicāra*) are subsumed within the three times, arise from causes and conditions, and so forth, up to following after various desires and the like.

One observes that the first dhyāna is accompanied by the movement of vitarka and vicāra, lacks tranquility, follows after the various desires, and only partially encompasses the joy and bliss born of seclusion.
Regarding the third passage, it says:
"The predominance of dwelling in suffering."

Tài says: Because the five aggregates and four aggregates inhabited by sentient beings of the lower realms are characterized by an increase in suffering, they are called "abodes of suffering. Jī says:
This means that the lower stages abide in the intensification of suffering.
Furthermore, herein, for those who have abandoned desire, the eight meditative absorptions (dhyāna) are extensively explained in two parts;
among these, the first explains the eight absorptions.
Subsequently, the distinctions will be clarified by contrasting them with the dhyānas and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*).

Regarding the first of these, the initial explanation concerns the first dhyāna: "Detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, possessing directed thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and experiencing the joy and bliss born of seclusion, one enters and dwells fully established in the dhyāna."
Regarding "the two desires and the two renunciations":
craving is termed the desire for affliction (*kleśa-kāma*),
while the five sense objects are termed the desire for things (*vastu-kāma*).
When the antidote arises, its concomitance with non-attachment is called "concomitant detachment.
Its aversion toward the five sensory objects is called "detachment from the objective sphere.
As for the term "detachment," it refers to having already attained the mental attention that culminates the stage of application (*prayoganiṣṭhā-manasikāra*).
Because one attains the ninth path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*),
one is able to abandon all unwholesome dharmas; therefore,
it is called "separation" (*vairāgya*).
Regarding what is called "arising," it is so termed because it arises immediately following this as its cause and condition;
regarding what is called "separation from arising," it is so termed because one attains the ninth uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) whereby desire and evil are completely eliminated.
Immediately following this, one attains the mental attention (*manasikāra*) that constitutes the fruit of the culmination of that preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Simultaneously, joy and bliss arise.
Regarding the statement "joy and bliss," it means that one has already attained the object sought after, and so forth.
Jingyun: "Joy" (*sukha*) refers to the feeling of pleasure (*saumanasya*), not to the [mental] factor of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
This means that this feeling of pleasure causes the body to experience a sense of well-being and satisfaction, which is termed "joy."
Master Ji says:
This refers to those of sharp faculties who, in the ninth path of liberation,
enter the fundamental dhyānas.
Therefore, it is said that "joy and bliss arise.
For a person of dull faculties, only after the ninth path of liberation within the preparatory concentration (sāmantaka-dhyāna) can they enter the fundamental dhyāna and give rise to joy and bliss.
Regarding the phrase "able to dwell correctly for as long as seven days and seven nights," Master Ji states:
"This clarifies that one can enter meditative absorption and remain therein for seven days and seven nights."
As for why it does not say "for a long time" but only "seven days" and so forth:
it is because in the desire realm, edible food is cut off for seven days;
if one remains in meditative absorption beyond seven days, the body will perish once one has emerged from that state.
Therefore, it cannot last for a long time.
Moreover, even if one attains such a state before entering the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), it does not endure for many months or years;
if more than seven days have passed since emerging from the absorption, the body will immediately perish.
If one emerges from meditative absorption within seven days, the body does not perish;
this discussion is based on the period before such perishing occurs, and thus it speaks only of "seven days.
Question: [Why is this so?]
After seven days have passed, he enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
If that were so, he would die upon emerging from the absorption.
The meaning is as follows:
This is not so. He does not die because he is sustained by the power of concentration from having entered meditative absorption for a long time;
nor does he die now, as he immediately enters a conscious state of absorption upon emerging from it.
Question: When emerging from the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti),
does the body perish or not perish because the absorption lacks sustaining power?
Answer: It is destroyed.
Next, regarding the explanation of "internal serenity" (*adhyātmasamprasāda*) within the second dhyāna:
This treatise is on faith.
When one attains the second dhyāna, one comes to know through faith that all afflictions belonging to the meditative stages can be abandoned;
therefore, faith becomes manifest.

In the Mahāyāna, the abandonment of discursive thought and investigation, along with distraction, through the application of equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, is termed "internal serenity.
Furthermore, because the mind of joy is agitated and leaping, it is not yet tranquil and thus cannot be designated as possessing equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension.
There is a textual passage regarding the twenty-seventh [topic]:
"That which is born of meditative concentration (dhyāna) differs from the first dhyāna."
That is called "born of detachment" (*vairāgyaja*), while this is called "born of concentration" (*samādhija*).
That is termed "born of detachment" because it first attains freedom from the fetters of the desire realm;
this is termed "born of concentration" because it relies on concentration already previously attained.
Regarding the statement, "As for 'joy and bliss,' it refers to having already attained the desired object and so forth":
in the first two dhyānas, both types of bliss are associated with the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*),
though they are conceptually distinguished as two.
If it causes the ālayavijñāna to experience a state of well-being, it is termed pleasure (*sukha*);
if it causes the manovijñāna to experience a state of well-being, it is termed joy (*prīti*).
One first seeks this joy and pleasure to cultivate the second dhyāna.
Now, the sought-after goal has been attained.
Tai says: "Examining the purport of this treatise, it appears that investigation and analysis (vitarka-vicāra) exist only within the preparatory concentration (anāgamya-samādhi)."
Therefore, while in the fundamental first dhyāna and the preparatory stage (anāgamya), vitarka and vicāra arise intermittently;
now, when attaining the second dhyāna, the preparatory means likewise lack vitarka and vicāra.
Hence, it is said that one "transcends" them.
Because it arises immediately after the fundamental first dhyāna as the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for the second dhyāna, it is called "born of concentration" (*samādhi-ja*).
Regarding the third dhyāna, equanimity (*upekṣā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*),
and clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*) all serve as remedies for joy (*prīti*).
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states that clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*) prevents the pleasure of one's own level [in the first dhyāna].
Xuanzang says:

"In both the first and second dhyānas, there is neither the pleasure of being free from joy (*prīti-vigata-sukha*) nor the pleasure of the mental consciousness aggregate (*manovijñāna-kalāpa*) being non-conceptual."
Although there is equanimity (upekṣā-vedanā), it arises alternately with joy (prīti) and applied and sustained thought (vitarka-vicāra), rather than being uninterrupted equanimity.
Baso (Kai) says:
"From the third dhyāna downward, there is no such bliss (sukha) nor uninterrupted equanimity."
That which follows is pleasure (*sukha*);
its essence is joy (*prīti*).
The distinction lies in its refreshing and gladdening the body and mind.
Now, within the third dhyāna, the mental state of satisfaction is also called "pleasure" (sukha) because pleasure reaches its ultimate limit there; therefore,
it is said that such pleasure does not exist in the lower stages.
Although equanimity exists within the lower stages, it is not specifically designated by that name;
furthermore, because there are interruptions, it is not uninterrupted equanimity, and thus it is said to be "non-existent."
It is not that there is an intermittent abandonment, nor is it that there is no name for such abandonment.
Regarding the explanation within the fourth dhyāna, it says:
"Furthermore, because the types of counteractive factors here are similar in their force, [they lead] up to causing one not to emerge from the superior bliss, etc., of the stage of the third dhyāna."
This commentary explains that within the lower three dhyānas, there are factors of antidote consisting of conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

Regarding the stage of the fourth dhyāna, however, it only explains the function of the antidote as being the abandonment of suffering and pleasure, without specifying the actual substance of that antidote.
Because it is similar in its category of counteractive power to the third dhyāna, it is omitted here;
however, the characteristics of the similar counteractives of the lower stages are briefly stated, namely:
equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension.
This refers to equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension within the stage of advancement in the third dhyāna;
because one feels aversion toward the pleasure of one's own level and seeks the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant,
it is therefore universally characterized by equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension.
If one is correctly emerging from that fourth dhyāna, the nature of the antidote consists solely of equanimity,
mindfulness, and clear comprehension,
because the lower pleasure has been eliminated.

It is said that because the power of the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) here is similar, the antidote consisting of the abandonment of pleasure (*sukha-prahāṇa*) is not explicitly taught; rather, only what is accomplished by the antidote—namely, the abandonment of pleasure and so forth—is taught. T’ai says:
What is called the category of counteragents for this fourth dhyāna?
It refers to equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension within the third dhyāna;
by repeatedly cultivating these very qualities within the third dhyāna, one enters the fourth dhyāna.
One is then able to relinquish the superior bliss within the third dhyāna,
because that superior bliss prevents the practitioner from emerging from the third dhyāna. Since this refers to the relinquishing of the means [of attainment],
it mentions only that which is to be abandoned (*pratipakṣya*) and does not mention the antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
For this reason, it is said in the Sūtra:
"By means of the abandonment of pleasure, one cultivates the fourth dhyāna;
at that very moment, all suffering and pleasure are transcended."

Because of the cause and condition for the cessation of pleasure and the cessation of pain in the fourth dhyāna, whether it be the cessation of pain in the first two dhyānas or the cessation of pleasure in the present fourth dhyāna, they are collectively summarized as:
"At the time of the fourth dhyāna, pleasure is abandoned and pain is abandoned; previously, joy and affection have subsided."
In that sutra, the character "first" (先) is used both upwardly and downwardly.
Upwardly, it refers to suffering being first severed; downwardly, it refers to sorrow and joy first vanishing.
Master Ji said:
In this context, equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension are called the antidotes;
the bliss of the third dhyāna is called the object to be countered.
Although the sūtra mentions only the bliss that is abandoned, it does not mention the equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension that abandon it.
Because the factors of equanimity, mindfulness, and so forth, which serve as antidotes in the third dhyāna,
are similar to these antidotal factors of this fourth dhyāna,
it is called a "type" (*jāti*); it is termed a "type" because its essential nature (*svabhāva*) is similar.
Because both are able to sever afflictions and are similar in these two respects, it is said that their power is similar; thus, [the sūtra] briefly omits further explanation.
This interpretation does not clarify the reason why the fourth antidote is not explicitly mentioned in the sūtra.
It is said that by repeatedly cultivating precisely this [equanimity], one is able to abandon [the delight in pleasure] so as not to remain within the third dhyāna.
Since the superior bliss within the stage of the third dhyāna is [pleasure], it is therefore stated: "by the abandoning of pleasure."
In this context, the pleasure bound to the third dhyāna fetters the practitioner,
preventing them from emerging from the third dhyāna and thereby obstructing their attainment of the superior fourth dhyāna therein.
Now, by repeatedly cultivating equanimity and mindfulness, one is able to relinquish this meditative pleasure.

It is said that "by reason of these causes and conditions, what was previously abandoned and what is now being abandoned are collectively described as 'the abandonment of pleasure and the abandonment of pain,' and the prior disappearance of sorrow and joy."
The pleasure associated with abandonment is called "abandoned now";
the remaining faculties of feeling are called "previously abandoned.
Therefore, the lower and middle [levels] are covered by the remedy, as it is said: "...up until the time one enters the first dhyāna, the feeling of sorrow (daurmanasya) has subsided."
Regarding this, as stated previously in the eleventh fascicle:
"For what reason is the faculty of suffering said to be not yet abandoned within the first dhyāna?
Because the heaviness (dausthulya) of that category has not yet been abandoned."
If it were in a body belonging to a lower realm, that would be possible.
For what reason, however, does the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) not manifest in one who dwells in the first dhyāna, even though it has not yet been abandoned?

This is because its associated counterparts—the various sufferings comprised within the faculty of mental grief (daurmanasyendriya)—have already been abandoned; only its underlying heaviness (dauṣṭhulya) remains unabandoned.

If the faculty of suffering were severed within the first dhyāna, then there would be no distinction in the meditative abidings resulting from the experience [of the second dhyāna] for a practitioner entering the first and second dhyānas;
for there would be no difference between the two, as both possess joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*).
It is only because the coarse and heavy [defilements] have not yet been abandoned that a distinction is said to exist.
Yet, the Sūtra states that there is a definite distinction based on emerging from the meditative absorptions (samāpatti) regarding the various feelings (vedanā).
A question is asked: "Is it not the case that a distinction is obtained simply through the abandonment or non-abandonment of vitarka and vicāra?"
Why must one necessarily sever the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) in order to speak of distinctions?
The meaning is this:
because applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) do not constitute mutual obstructions to joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*).
One cannot explain the distinction of joy (*prīti*) by means of the cessation of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).
Because the joy of the first dhyāna still possesses the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), its excellence has not yet been described.
Since the joy of the second dhyāna has already abandoned suffering, that joy is pure and superior.
If one were to explain the distinction by means of the conceptual investigations (*vitarka*) and discursive thoughts (*vicāra*) of existence and non-existence,
then since the phenomena of existence and non-existence are immeasurably diverse, how could their meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) be distinct?
Now, conversely, it would follow as a logical difficulty that the feelings of pleasure (*sukha*) and joy (*prīti*) must likewise lack any distinction.
Because the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) is identical in nature to joy, pleasure, and so forth as being a feeling (vedanā),
they mutually exclude one another. If the faculty of suffering were not excluded by the joy of the first and second dhyānas,
there would be no distinction between the joy and pleasure found in those two stages.
Since suffering had already been abandoned prior to the first dhyāna, what is abandoned here is the coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*);
it is not said that its seeds are abandoned,
for they still exist in the Arhat.

Regarding the "sphere of infinite space" (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), Master Jing explains: because one gives rise to resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding space, one first transcends the perceptions associated with visual consciousness that apprehend blue, yellow, and so forth;

next, one transcends the perceptions of resistance associated with auditory consciousness, tactile consciousness—which respectively take the five sense organs as their objects—and mental consciousness.
The third [type of perception] occurs below the fourth dhyāna, taking as its objects various signs such as food, drink, vessels, and clothing within the desire realm;

it continues until the text below states: "It should be known that herein, based on the preparatory concentration (*sāmantaka*) and not yet having entered the fundamental [dhyāna], one takes only space and so forth as the object."
This text clearly states that the name of the "emptiness-sphere concentration" (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi*) is derived from its preparatory means (*upāya*).

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "within the access concentrations (*sāmantaka*), one also takes as an object all the aggregates belonging to the lower stages," this refers to the practice of observing the visible forms (*rūpa*) within the fourth dhyāna and other levels as being blue, yellow, and so forth.

Based on this, there is the form of mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi-vaśitā-rūpa*). Tai [Xuanzang] explains that "surpassing" is distinguished in terms of manifest color (*varṇa-rūpa*), while "having the perception of resistance" (*sapratigha-saṃjñā*) is spoken of in terms of visible form (*dṛśya-rūpa*).
Regarding "the perception of variety" (*nānātva-saṃjñā*), Ji [Daoxuan] states: "Within those various aggregates, even when mental attention does not function, and so forth."

This refers to when one whose body is situated in the desire realm intends to rely upon space; at that time, as one eliminates the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*), one also eliminates the objects of form within the desire realm.
Therefore, it is said that "one abandons the perception of villages, armies, and so forth."

It is not that one born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) desires to enter space and thus performs this rejection; rather, it should be understood that the subsequent passage here describes it as follows: [The text continues: "It is not that one born in the form realm desires to enter space and thus performs this rejection. From the fourth dhyāna upward, among these nine paths of liberation, the seventh mental application exists only within the fundamental meditative absorptions (*mauladhyāna*).
At the single moment of its initial attainment, this path of liberation takes as its object only the aggregates (*skandha*) of its own level.
The mind of the second moment takes as its object the aggregates (*skandha*) of the higher and lower stages;
however, since this is explained here with reference to the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) of the very first moment, it is said that it also takes the aggregates of its own stage as its object.
If the nine uninterrupted paths (*ānantaryamārga*) of the preparatory concentrations (*sāmantaka*) take only the lower stages as their object because they produce revulsion,
it is said that they also take all the aggregates (*skandha*) belonging to the lower stages as their object;
their first eight paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), however, take the aggregates of both the upper and lower stages as their objects.
Since this is explained here in reference to the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga), it is said that they also take the aggregates (skandha) of the lower stages as objects;

however, this does not exclude the fact that [the paths of liberation] take as their objects the aggregates of the neighboring stages (sāmantaka), the fundamental stages (maula), and their own respective stages, whether above, below, or on the same level.

Regarding the preparatory concentrations (*sāmantaka*), since the treatise does not mention nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) among the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), it is said that they take the aggregates of the lower stage as their object.

Regarding the fundamental concentrations (*maula-dhyāna*), because the first moment is mentioned while the second moment and those following are omitted, it is said that they also take the aggregates of their own stage as their object.
Therefore, the treatise does not state that [the path] takes only the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth of its own level as its object, but rather says it "also" takes them as its object.
This uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and liberation path (*vimukti-mārga*) are to be understood as previously explained in the section on the first dhyāna.
If this contradicts the second fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*,
as that text explains according to the interpretation of the Great Master,
it describes three types of persons who attain the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) based on the exegesis of the Tripiṭaka.
First, when a noble one attains entry into the fundamental dhyāna, they universally take as objects the higher stages, their own stage, and space.
Second, when an ordinary person within [the realm] enters the fundamental dhyāna, they take the higher stages and space as objects due to the power of prior hearing and cultivation.

Third, when non-Buddhists enter that fundamental meditative absorption (*maula-samādhi*), although they take space as their object along with the four aggregates of themselves and others, they do not take a higher stage as their object; for they reckon this concentration on space to be the ultimate fruit.
Now, this is stated specifically in response to the non-Buddhists (tīrthika).
The masters of the Abhidharma (Abhidharmika) also provide this interpretation within their explanation of the sphere of consciousness (vijñānāyatana).
That is to say, when one intends to practice the contemplation of the infinity of consciousness,
one first contemplates the sphere of infinite space based on the preparatory stage (sāmantaka) of the sphere of infinite consciousness;
since the space being contemplated is already boundless, [one then proceeds to the sphere of infinite consciousness].
The consciousness that takes emptiness as its object is likewise boundless.
Consequently, one observes that the consciousness of that stage is also boundless.
Upon entering the fundamental station of consciousness, one then comprehensively observes the four aggregates and the four types of consciousness of that same stage.
Regarding the resolution of non-existence within the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*):

it refers to the conceptual resolution that while the sphere of nothingness actually consists of the four aggregates along with the matter of mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi-vaśitā-rūpa*), there is nevertheless a total absence of any other objective domain.
Therefore, there is conceptual resolution (*adhimukti*) and conceptual attention (*manasikāra*).
Apart from consciousness, there is not even the slightest objective realm (*ālambana*).
Thus it is said that "there is not even the slightest thing," which means one forms the resolution that there is no object.
The manifestation of the mind as existence and non-existence is subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states that the principle of ultimate reality is not subsumed under the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
That which manifests as mind is not subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Regarding the "Peak of Existence" (*bhavāgra*),
according to the interpretation of Master Jing, it is called "non-perception" (*asaṃjñin*) because it transcends the two types of perception.
First, the perception of existence;
second, the perception of non-existence.
Because one transcends the sphere of infinite consciousness and below, there is the perception of existence, it is therefore said that "there may be the perception of existence."
Furthermore, because one has transcended the perception of the sphere of nothingness, it is said that "there may be the perception of nothingness.
Being devoid of those two perceptions is called "the perception of neither-existence-nor-non-existence."
Because it possesses subtle perception— unlike the two mindless absorptions where all perceptions are entirely absent—
it is called "not non-perception.
As for the statement that it "proceeds by taking the object of non-perception as its condition":
This means that because the objective sphere (ālambana-viṣaya) of the mind of non-perception lacks coarse characteristics, it is called "taking the signless as its object" (*animitta-ālambana*).
It does not mean that taking only the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) as an object is what is meant by "taking the signless as its object.
Master Ji’s explanation of this contains three points.
First, to correctly clarify the arousal of the higher meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), one regards the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) as a coarse characteristic (*audārikanimitta*).
This refers to the entire sequence from "furthermore" (*punar api*) up until "one is able to relinquish the perception of the sphere of nothingness."
The second part explains the name "Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.
Within this, there are two sections;
first is the explanation of "not having perception."
Second, it clarifies that this is not the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñin*).

From the point where it says, "By this cause and condition, when first entering the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*)," down to "or there may be the perception of something existing, or the perception of nothing existing," it explains that this is not the state of having perception (*saṃjñin*).
From the sphere of infinite consciousness downward, there is the perception of "something existing.
In the sphere of nothingness, there is the perception of "nothing existing.
Therefore, it is said that "neither-perception" refers to neither the perception of something existing nor the perception of nothing existing.
Now, within the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), there are not the former two types of perception (*saṃjñā*).
It is not that among those with perception there are two kinds of having perception;
nor is it that within those without perception there are two kinds of being without perception.
Therefore, within the second major section, the second time it clarifies that [the state] is not "non-conception" (asaṃjñin).
There are two types of non-conception:
first, the attainment of non-conception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti).
Second is the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). In these two attainments, the mind is entirely extinguished;
however, this is not the case for the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Therefore, it is said that they are not "without perception" (asaṃjñin);
this refers precisely to the two types of the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti).
This is because within the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), there exists a subtle form of perception.

The third [section] clarifies that at the time of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), one transcends the lower levels such as the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and its own preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) to enter the fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*). This refers to the following passage: "When one gives rise to resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) within this very state... and so forth.
Regarding the third explanation concerning the two mindless absorptions (*acittaka-samāpatti*),
Master Jing’s commentary and interpretation states:
"The first [point] pertains to the difference between the entry into the two absorptions by the two types of individuals."

Thus, regarding these two attainments, the following passage clarifies the difference in the timing of the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for cultivating them through two types of mental attention (*manasikāra*):

namely, that the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is entered by cultivating a gradual abandonment through the mental attention of revulsion toward perception and the mental attention of perceiving it as liberation.

If, from a state of mind characterized by compassion and perception, one seeks to progress further, then as the mind progresses upward, it seeks an upper object of focus but ultimately finds nothing to be obtained.

Because nothing is obtained, one then engages in mental attention toward the cessation of sensation and perception for a time; from coarse to subtle, the nine grades [of consciousness] gradually cease, and having ceased, they do not recur.
Regarding these two meditative attainments, the attainment of cessation first arises within a body belonging to the desire realm;
for it is by relying on the teaching and practicing according to the teaching that one first attains it within the desire realm.
Subsequently, those who dwell in the four dhyānas and are born in the four formless realms (ārūpyadhātu) all attain the subsequent arising [of the fruit].
Regarding the attainment of non-conceptualization (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), the *Ṣaṭtriṃśat-sāhasra-sarvāstivāda-vinaya-ksudraka* (or *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya*, Chapter 6, Verse 3) states:
First arising in this [desire realm] and subsequently arising again in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"The initial arising of the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) in both realms pertains to both determinate and indeterminate karma, whether prior or subsequent."
The Mahāyāna section on karma clarifies that the three periods of karma, as well as indeterminate karma, all encompass both determinate and indeterminate types.
According to the explanatory text below,
when any Arhat is about to enter the state of nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), they must necessarily enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
The six consciousnesses cease and the mind dwells solely in the ālayavijñāna at the moment of death.

Jì (Jizang) says: "In this way, those in training who have already abandoned the craving for the sphere of nothingness and so forth" refers to the attainment of realization through the severance of afflictions.
Other passages state that "only those in the desire realm first give rise to the attainment of cessation.
This refers to the basis of the teaching;
when first training, one must necessarily rely upon the desire realm.
When it first arises later, one also attains it in the form realm,
as in the case of a person who has attained the third fruit;
previously, while in the desire realm, they had not yet attained this concentration.
One attains this meditative absorption only after having been born in the form realm;
thus, it is first produced [there].
However, because one first heard this teaching in the desire realm and was subsequently born in the form realm, [the absorption arises there].
Fourth, regarding the discernment of the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*):
first, a brief explanation.
One must have already attained the fundamental dhyānas (*mauladhyāna*) beforehand.
Subsequently, one relies upon the correct Dharma for cultivating supernatural powers through hearing and upholding it;
first, one relies upon the mental attention of hearing and reflection to engage in contemplation,
and next, one relies upon the mental attention of the stage of meditative concentration to comprehend the meaning and the teachings.
By comprehending the meaning of the Dharma, one cultivates and purifies the mind, thereby giving rise to the fruit of cultivation.
Regarding the phrase "at times" (*kadācit*) used by Tai [Shi]:
"times" (*kāla*) refers to a brief duration.
It should be stated that "at times, the fruit of cultivation arises.
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "In this way, having understood the meaning and the phenomena" constitutes the second extensive explanation.
Within this, first there is a general enumeration of the twelve perceptions;
next, a detailed explanation;
and finally, a summary of how the cultivation of these perceptions induces the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and so forth.
Within the detailed explanation,
the twelve [bases] are categorized into five groups;
based on the first five perceptions, one cultivates the supernormal power of the divine realm (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*).
Based on the sixth perception, one cultivates the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives;
based on the seventh perception, one cultivates the supernormal knowledge of the divine ear;
and based on the eighth perception of light, one cultivates the supernormal knowledge of the death and rebirth of beings.
Based on the ninth perception, one cultivates the distinction of mental training for the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);

based on the subsequent liberations, spheres of mastery, and spheres of totality, one cultivates the three perceptions that can induce the various noble supernormal powers, as well as the merit of inducing the absence of strife (*araṇā*), the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*), and the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
"Like tūla-cotton" refers to the cocoon of the wild silkworm, which is called tūla-cotton.
Furthermore, according to the custom of the Western lands, much grass is spread upon the ground to serve as a seat.
Alternatively, it is like a skilled practitioner who,
when wishing to card wool for weighing, possesses the characteristic of carding wool;
this is called "mastery," wherein body and mind are in harmonious accord.
Master Ji says that both the body and the mind can undergo transformation.
If it is a transformation of the body, it is the karma of the body;
if it is a transformation of the mind, it is the transformative mind.

Regarding "the perception of resolute conviction" (*adhimukti-saṃjñā*): this refers to the intention of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* concerning resolving upon what is distant as being near, and so forth.
Jinamitra states: "Resolving upon what is distant" means...
This refers to perceiving the long as short and the near as distant;
it is the distortion of the short into the long and the confusion between the coarse and the subtle.
This is the transformation of the physical substance;
earth and water act upon one another.
This is the transformation of the four great elements.
In this context, only the two transformations of form and sound are mentioned,
without discussing the other sense objects,
as explained in detail in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*.
Regarding the phrase "or manifesting many bodies from a single body by means of the perception of transformative resolve":
it refers to one who originally possesses only a single body further manifesting many bodies through the mind of transformation.
The supernormal power of transformation is subsumed under the supernormal power of the miraculous domain (*ṛddhiviṣaya*).
Alternatively, regarding the statement that "one manifests as a single body from many bodies by means of the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) of concealment and transformation":
previously, one manifested many bodies.
Now, by means of the resolve for concealment, they hide many transformation bodies and leave only a single body;
these two are accomplished through the perception of resolve.
Alternatively, they pass straight through walls and other obstacles without impediment, even treading upon them as if they were the ground.
This is accomplished through the perception of the space element (*ākāśadhātu*), or like a bird in flight;
this is accomplished through the perception of lightness and flexibility.

Regarding "having mastery over the transformation of a portion of the derived matter (bhautika-rūpa) produced by the four great elements (mahābhūta) in the Brahma-world," Jing says that while derived matter generally comprises ten categories,
here it refers specifically to the transformation of the sense-object of visible form (rūpāyatana).
It may be of the same class as that [derived matter] or of a different class;
therefore, it is called "a portion of derived matter.
Tai says: "The two kinds of transformation" refers to this.
First, the person possessing supernormal powers (ṛddhi) can come and go with ease.
Second, they are able to transform a portion of the derived matter (bhautika-rūpa) of the Brahma-world,
freely changing it into blue or yellow, and likewise transforming a portion of all speech.
Master Ji says: "A portion" refers to the two kinds of derived matter—namely, visible form and sound—and thus it is called "a portion.
It is called "a portion" because it consists only of external objects, such as non-reactive tangibles and the five sense organs.
Furthermore, because that which is transformed according to meditative concentration consists only of two parts and a portion of one part,
and because it cannot transform the entirety of the Brahma-world, it is said to be "a portion.
This refers to the sixth [type of] perception.
"Cloud" refers to that which, by means of this perception, revolves according to recollection from the stage of childhood up until the present.
