As stated in the *Abhidharma-śāstra*, the supernormal power of recollecting past lives first deduces from the current body—starting from old age—back through middle age, youth, childhood, and infancy.
Up to this point, it has been established that the previous life constitutes the *pūrvanivāsa* (past abodes) at the moment of death;
as for the current statement that [the sequence] extends from the stage of childhood up to the present,
this is said in reference to the distant preparatory conditions (*dūraprayoga*).
If it is established by subsequent moments of thought,
then one should gradually trace back from the present body until one reaches the aggregates at the moment of death.
The recollection of past lives is only fully accomplished when one remembers and understands the successive sequence of previous actions without omission.
This refers to the initial stage of cultivation, which requires proceeding in order from the most recent toward the past.
If one knows them with emphasis,
one knows them all either in sequential order or by skipping;
this occurs within the seventh perception.
The assembly that has gathered at the designated place for the purpose of deliberation is called the "assembly of the meaning of the city" (*nagaramaṇḍalī*) or the "vast and extensive assembly."
Tài says there are two interpretations regarding the "West":
first, a marketplace;
second, a place for children to play.
The foundation is likewise the same.
Furthermore, it is explained that this is because the location is vast and extensive.
The multitude is also immeasurable;
"many" is intended here to mean a great number.
This refers to the eighth perception.

That is to say: when obstructed by walls or mountains, or at an extremely distant place, one forms the perception of light to illuminate the object of knowledge, forming the perception of seeing it clearly.

Furthermore, one takes up the supernormal power of knowledge regarding birth and death (*jāti-maraṇa-jñāna-abhijñā*), which brings about the attainment of pleasure and pain based on good and evil, and leads to the cultivation [of this power].
Seeing those sentient beings dying here and there and being born in various states through various means, it is named after its object.
Within the ninth perception,
this refers to discerning the transformations of the physical forms of sentient beings who possess desire and so forth.
Because one cultivates this extensively, the fruit of cultivation arises as a specific knowledge of the mind;
it is named after its object and also named after its functional capacity.
T'ai says: "Regarding the affairs and principles of sentient beings, there is darkness and obscurity in all respects."
Therefore, it is said that the meaning of the matters is obscure;
the words issuing from their mouths are not what the world esteems,
and they constantly employ vulgar speech without any authoritative foundation.
Therefore, it is called "vulgar.
In the latter three contemplations, the text is divided into two parts:
first, it explains the cultivation of the three contemplations by citing the supernormal powers and other qualities of the noble ones.
Regarding the subsequent discussion on the distinctions between the noble and the non-noble based on their mutual correspondence:
within the preceding [section],
there is the explanation of the notions of liberation (vimokṣa), the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), and the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana).
That is to say: the perception of external forms while having the internal conception of form;
the perception of external forms while lacking the internal conception of form;
and the perception of pure forms, such as blue, yellow, and so forth, while lacking the internal conception of form.
In some cases, within the *abhibhvāyatana* (bases of mastery), one contemplates internal formlessness while perceiving external forms as limited, and so forth;
or, within the *kṛtsnāyatana* (bases of totality), one contemplates the pervasive perception of blue, yellow, and so on.
Because one has approached, cultivated, and practiced these perceptions extensively, [they arise].
It can remove all obstacles that obstruct the superknowledges (abhijñā) and can induce the most excellent supernormal powers of the noble ones,
whether they be the power of transformation, the power of creation, or the power of resolute conviction (adhimokṣa).
Transformation (*pariṇāma*) refers to the universal essence;
metamorphosis (*nirmāṇa*) refers to the universal fruit.
It is also termed supernormal power (*abhijñā*).
One who possesses mastery through resolute conviction perceives the distant as near;
by contracting and extending their arms and neck, they reach as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
Furthermore, the conceptualization of earth as water and so forth is called "resolute conviction" (adhimokṣa).
This includes the absence of conflict (araṇā), the knowledge resulting from prayer (praṇidhijñāna), and the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid).
Furthermore, it is through the cultivation of the perception of liberation and so forth that one is able to accomplish this by eliminating delusion regarding the objective sphere.
It may also be that a thing undergoes a transformation of its state, which is termed "reversal."
That which is non-existent suddenly acquires a name;
this is superior to the previous explanation.
Below, the differences are distinguished in contrast.
The *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* is likewise.
Regarding certain distinct meanings, the transformation of ordinary beings does not exceed seven days,
whereas for noble ones (*ārya*), it may exceed that.
One may cite that treatise; hereafter,
the summary concludes by following the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*,
which states that all five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are mundane knowledge (*laukika-jñāna*).
Furthermore, that which is attained by those in training (śaikṣa) is with outflows (sāsrava),
because their outflows have not yet been exhausted;
whereas that which is attained within the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is free from outflows.
It is also called "untainted" (*anāsrava*).
Regarding the fifth section, which clarifies the distinctions among the places of birth resulting from the cultivation of worldly pure concentrations (*laukika-śuddha-samādhi*), Jing says:
The commentary states: The three heavens of the first dhyāna are named according to their freedom from the defilement of desire;
they are all termed "Brahma."
The second three heavens are named according to the strength or weakness of their bodily radiance.
The third three heavens...
The fourth dhyāna is so named because the pure bliss obtained therein pervades the entire body rather than just parts of it;
it is the realm where the celestial stars are arrayed and where there is no ground of clouds.
First, it obtained its name as the Heaven of No Clouds (Anabhraka).
Second, it was named after the most excellent field of merit (puṇyakṣetra).
The third [classification] is named after the fruits attained.
Next are the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).
Because those who have cultivated mixed karma through untainted (*anāsrava*) practice are born in these five pure places, they are so called.
In the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space, according to the distinctions among three types of persons who cultivate inferior, middling, and superior goodness,
they will respectively experience the three fruits upon being born in the sphere of infinite space;
this applies likewise up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
They are called the "Devas Who Follow" because those deities have neither form nor color, nor do they have a fixed location;
rather, their distinctions consist solely in their respective abodes.
Regarding the four dhyānas, one attains retribution according to whether the practice performed was superior, middling, or inferior, thereby being born in those respective heavens.
Because the excellence or inferiority of the retribution obtained follows the quality of the practice, they are called "Heavens Following Practice" (Anulomika-deva). Master Ji said:
The first dhyāna heaven is named Brahmā; "Brahmā" has the meaning of purity.
Because it is the first state to be free from desire, it receives the name "Pure.
The second dhyāna is named "Radiant."
It receives the name "Radiant" because it is initially free from applied and sustained thought;
the third dhyāna receives the name "Pure" because it attains superior bliss.
Supreme Bliss (Abhyudaya) is called "Pure" (Śuddha).
In the fourth dhyāna, ordinary beings and sages dwell together in three heavens;
the first is named Cloudless (Anabhraka).
The others are named according to the increase of their merit;
thus, the names of the five Śuddhāvāsa heavens are explained, and so forth.
This concludes the explanation of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Regarding the phrase "among the homogeneous class of the gods who follow their conduct":
in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there are no distinct places for receiving retribution;
rather, one receives this retribution immediately according to the three grades of conduct.
Therefore, they are called "gods who follow their conduct.
However, regarding the distinctions in their activities while dwelling [there],
it means that there are differences in the karmic actions performed during their three stages of existence.
Now, this textual passage is consistent with the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*:
one cultivates the three grades of karma within the first dhyāna and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*),
yet receives no distinct fruit.
The latter three dhyānas, according to the cultivation of the three grades of karma,
receive distinct results.
The sixth [point] clarifies the one who is free from desire.
Within the marks, there are thirteen marks;
one may cite the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (Treatise on Knowledge) to discern their similarities or differences.
From here below, the second section explains the transition to the supramundane.
Within this, first there is the connection between what precedes and what follows;
next, the seven types of mental attention are distinguished;
and finally, there is a summary conclusion.
Regarding the statement in the preceding section that one gradually gives rise to the seven types of attention (*manasikāra*) and eventually realizes the fruit of arhatship:
during the first three preparatory stages (*prayoga*), one cultivates the attention that discerns the characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī-manasikāra*).
One personally realizes the various characteristics, such as the four truths and the sixteen aspects;

among the four roots of merit, one cultivates the mental application of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*), because the path of seeing is proximate to the mind of resolute conviction and thus cultivates the practice of the truths therein.
In the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one cultivates the mental application of detachment (*viveka-manasikāra*),
which is able to exhaust the afflictions of seeing (*darśana-heya-kleśa*).
In the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one cultivates the mental application of joy in gathering (*ratisaṃgrāhaka-manasikāra*).

The stage from the commencement of abandoning the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation— attaining the two intermediate fruits and abandoning the afflictions of the form and formless realms,
up until the eighth uninterrupted path of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception— is the stage of the mental application of "delight in cultivation" (*ratisaṃprayukta-manaskāra*).
The attention of investigation (mīmāṃsā-manaskāra) is able to observe and know, within the stage of cultivation, those points where defilements have been abandoned and those where they have not;
it abandons the delusions regarding non-perception (asaṃjñika).
The diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi), which is the ninth path of immediate succession (ānantarya-mārga), is the attention of the culmination of application (prayoga-niṣṭhā-manaskāra).
The knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising constitute the fruit of the culmination of the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Although the text employs provisional characteristics to make such distinctions,
in reality, there are seven types of mental attention (*manasikāra*) throughout these stages.
Regarding the second section, which distinguishes the sequence of the arising of the cultivation of the seven mental attentions (*manasikāra*),
if one were to judge according to the four lines of the verse, it should be divided into four parts;
however, based on this current text, the sequence of the cultivation of the seven mental attentions is explained.
This constitutes seven sections.
First is the attention consisting of the discernment of characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*), which contains two parts.

First, a brief analysis of practicing according to the teachings, wherein the sixteen aspects that comprehend the characteristics of the four noble truths are called the "aspects of comprehension" (*lakṣaṇa-prativedha*).
Second, an extensive analysis of the sixteen aspects that comprehend the characteristics of the four noble truths.
In the preceding [section],
each of the truths was individually explained with both definition and exposition;
because it is complete with both definition and exposition, it is called "well-spoken."

Furthermore, another interpretation is that among the three turnings of the Dharma wheel, the wheel of the Four Noble Truths is called the "concise summary," while those from the second turning onward are called the "detailed exposition."

Regarding the phrase "having already well-cultivated the mental attention (*manasikāra*) in [the preliminary stage]," this means that within the *anāgamya* (preliminary) concentration, one has already well-cultivated mental attention, or has attained the fundamental dhyānas or the formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
Regarding the second section, the "Extensive Explanation," it is divided into two parts.
First, the individual explanation of the sixteen aspects through which the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths are realized; second, the manifestation of the stages and levels (*bhūmi*).
Within the former, there are three subsections.
First, it clarifies the observation of the Four Truths of the desire realm;
second, it clarifies the observation of the Four Truths of the higher realms;

third, one should know that this concludes by summarizing that these two types of knowledge are the basis for the seeds from which the subsequent knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge of categories (*anvayajñāna*) arise.
In the beginning and middle [of this section], there is first a detailed explanation followed by a summary.
Within the former, there are four parts;
the first explains the Truth of Suffering, which is divided into three sections.
First, the ten practices are presented as the means for awakening to and entering the four practices;
second, the ten practices are explained individually as they enter the four practices;
finally, the ten practices are summarized as being subsumed within the four practices.
Within the detailed explanation,
first there is a summary of the ten practices as being observed through the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), followed by the detailed explanation itself.
This explanation is divided into four parts.
The first five lines constitute the practice of realizing impermanence (*anityatā*).
The subsequent three lines consist of the practices of realizing suffering (*duḥkha*), namely the three types of sensation: pleasant, painful, and neutral sensations.
Entering the practice of emptiness through the practice of non-apprehension;
entering the practice of selflessness through the practice of lack of autonomy.
This is divided into four parts at the beginning.
The first two modes of practice are explained together,
because the latter three modes are explained separately and in sequence.
Regarding the first:
One contemplates impermanence by means of the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Regarding the first, in clarifying reliance on the authority of the scriptures (*āptāgama-pramāṇa*), it says:
"As explained at length in the *Saptasūryodaya-sūtra*," which refers to the *Kalpa-sūtra*.
Because it explains the events of the seven days, it is called the *Saptāha-sūtra*.
Next, it clarifies that direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) gives rise to faith based on the teachings,
thereby attaining certainty regarding the practice of impermanence (*anityatā*).
By the power of such predominant faith, one repeatedly investigates and examines that all presently perceived things are not entirely devoid of the nature of impermanence;
that is to say, one first establishes two categories: internal and external phenomena.
The internal refers to the six sense bases and so forth; external things consist of sixteen types as listed in the text.
Among these, there are fifteen kinds of internal transformations of activity, also as listed in the text.
Furthermore, there are eight kinds of causes and conditions for transformation, which are also listed as in the text.
In the subsequent explanation,
the eight kinds of causes and conditions for transformation are explained by proceeding from the end toward the beginning.
Next, having explained the fifteen transformations of internal phenomena, one explains the sixteen kinds of transformations of external phenomena.
Within the explanation of the causes and conditions for eight of these transformations, it says:
"That which is fanned and heated by the wind."
Regarding the phrase "a great wind blowing upon wet clothes and so forth," this refers to when there are wet clothes,
or perhaps a wet ground.
Alternatively, it refers to when crops and the like are fanned by great winds, causing the water to dry up and the plants to wither.
"𥌁" (pronounced *chū*, with the initial sound of *diǎn*) means as urgent as the worldly expression "this is extremely parched. It signifies that [the moisture] has been completely dried up.
The lower summary:
All transformations of internal and external phenomena, whether material or immaterial, arise from these eight kinds of causes and conditions.
This concludes the explanation of the fifteen internal matters.
Regarding the expression "dry speech" (*kangyu*):
Tai and Ji both explain that it refers to speaking when one is hot; thus, at the time of speaking, the mouth becomes dry.
It is like what people in the world say: "dry speech, moist laughter."
"Crouching and contorted" refers to one who,

through contact with a touch conducive to pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanīya-sparśa*), experiences the pleasure arising from that condition, and is at that time capable of discerning the state of the pleasant feeling for oneself.
Master Ji said:
"For now, we shall cite only pleasant contact (*sukha-vedanīya-spraṣṭavya*) and not yet cite painful contact (*duḥkha-vedanīya-spraṣṭavya*) and so forth;
therefore it is said: 'By means of encountering a contact conducive to pleasant feeling.'"
This refers specifically to sensations such as suffering and so forth.
Regarding "experiencing pleasure when it arises conditioned by a pleasant contact":
the "pleasant contact" refers to the object that is capable of producing a pleasant contact.

Now, when the mental discourse apprehends an object that accords with a pleasant touch and pleasure arises, one is able to know for oneself that this is the state of a pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*).
Regarding the sixteen external objects, Jing says:
The first six types are the objects to be appropriated;
the latter ten types are the objects that serve as the body's requisites.
Regarding the six types that are the objects to be appropriated:
That is to say: first, the matter of the earth;
second, the matter of the encircling mountains; third, the matter of the mountains.
Fourth, matters concerning water;
fifth, matters concerning occupations;
sixth, matters concerning storehouses.
The ten types of bodily requisites are:
first, the matter of drink;
second, the matter of food.
Third, matters concerning the three vehicles;
fourth, matters concerning clothing;
fifth, matters concerning ornaments.
Sixth, matters concerning dance, song, music, and so forth;
seventh, matters concerning perfumes and garlands;
eighth, matters concerning requisites.
Ninth, matters of light and darkness;
tenth, matters of male and female.
If one relies on the aforementioned list of names:
Food and drink are each distinct matters;
now, within this explanation, food and drink are combined into a single explanation,
following the method of combining explanations into one.
Third, regarding the observation of impermanence through inference:
it is said that one observes the nature of impermanence as transformation precisely by the power of the dominant mental attention (*adhipati-manasikāra*) arising from such direct perception.
This passage concludes the preceding section.
From the phrase "up to 'one should correctly infer'" onwards,
it clarifies that the great destruction and dissolution of all phenomena, such as form and so forth, are easy to understand.
Arising and ceasing moment by moment are difficult to perceive because they are so subtle;
now, wishing to analyze this, I shall first initiate the discussion.
How does one infer that which is below?
This correctly analyzes subtle impermanence;
herein there are two parts.
First, the coarse is used to infer the subtle;
second, the presently experienced fruit is used to infer the past, unperceived cause.
Regarding the former, I rely on the explanation of Master Jigong.
Therefore, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) must necessarily possess momentary arising and ceasing;
it is because there is this small, subtle arising and ceasing that one attains the great transformational arising and ceasing.
It is not that a phenomenon which is not fixed by nature undergoes transformation;
nor is it that one perceives great arising and ceasing through the observation of minor arising and ceasing.

Rather, because things exist due to the conjunction of various conditions, they naturally perish from the moment they have arisen until the point where they no longer require external causes and conditions for their destruction.
The commentary clarifies the refutation of the objection by stating that cessation has causes and conditions.
Specifically, it addresses the objection:
"Do you not know that both arising and cessation possess causes and conditions?"
Now, it is generally said:
this dharma arises because of the convergence of various conditions;
thus, arising itself possesses causes and conditions.
It does not perish spontaneously due to causes and conditions;
that is, the dharma of cessation is without causes and conditions.
From such existing causes and conditions of transformation until the point where [the dharma] is no longer produced.
The commentary clarifies the anticipated objection.
The anticipated objection states:
"In this way, the sun's heat causes green leaves to turn yellow."
One might ask: "Does this green leaf not fail to appear as green because of the sun?
Is it not the case that the sun is the condition for the destruction of its greenness?
To this, the present commentary replies:
The sun can transform blue into yellow.
Thus, why do you say that the sun is merely a causal condition for change?
This very sun is the causal condition for the subsequent arising of the yellow color.
The preceding blue color is not the causal condition for its destruction. Why is this?
Because it is directly perceived by worldly people that after the preceding blue color has ceased, yellow arises.
This yellow and the blue are not similar;
it can be established that this yellow arises from existence.
Therefore, we know that the sun serves as the condition for the arising of the yellow, and not the cessation of the blue as its condition.
If, after the green has been scorched by the sun and no longer arises, the sun can serve as the condition for the destruction of the green,
and if there is a condition for destruction such that the subsequent yellow arises,
then it is clearly known that the sun serves as the condition for the arising of the subsequent yellow.
The destruction of blue is not the condition [for its non-apprehension].
It is not the case that everything becomes unapprehendable because of it; for if blue were destroyed, all subsequent phenomena would not entirely become unapprehendable.
Rather, on that very day, the destruction of blue serves as the condition.
The sub-commentary explains as follows:
"From 'there being some conditioned phenomena that have already perished' up to 'they are also no longer obtainable,' this is the objection raised by the opponent."
If, after this has ceased, another dharma arises, it may be understood as before.
But if, after this dharma has ceased, no other dharma arises,
how then is this to be explained?
When boiling water, it is completely exhausted; there is no remaining for future conditions and so forth.
Thus, one knows that the phenomenon of cessation possesses causes and conditions.
Regarding the statement that "those [beings] also, through a succession of causes and conditions, have come down to performing such actions until now," the Master of the Treatise explains:
"This is identical to the previous explanation."
In boiling water, both the fire and the water serve as conditions for the successive arising of subsequent phenomena.
When the water finally ceases to exist, it is not by means of the fire that the water is made to cease;
rather, the momentum of the water itself comes to an end, thereby causing the fire to lack the conditions for the arising of subsequent phenomena.
Therefore, the present cessation of dharmas likewise lacks causes and conditions. Jing says:
"It is due to the power of fire."
The former [fire] assists the increasing water,
while the latter [water] causes the subsequent water to diminish;
therefore, fire serves as the generative cause for the water that increases, in relation to the water that subsequently diminishes.
Each preceding instance of water, having arisen, ceases of its own accord without further depending on a cause;
this continues until the final momentary drop of water, which cannot act as a cause for the arising of a subsequent drop, but ceases spontaneously.
Therefore, when subsequent water fails to arise where it ought to arise,
it is called the "exhaustion of water.
The destruction of the vessel is likewise.
The meaning is the same as Master Ji’s explanation.
Ji further assisted in the objection, saying:
"The present day serves as the condition for the subsequent yellow sprout."
"Furthermore, would it not also serve as a condition for the preceding blue to cease? The answer is: No."
If a single causal condition were capable of producing both arising and ceasing,
then since arising and ceasing are mutually contradictory,
how could that which is contradictory be a single condition?
If the conditions that give rise [to a phenomenon] were one,
then the phenomena produced should likewise not be contradictory and should also be one.
Furthermore, if a ceasing phenomenon possessed causes and conditions, [it would follow that it could not cease].
That which exists through conditions is precisely that which undergoes cessation;
that which has ceased serves as a condition, and because it has conditions, it is able to arise.
Thus, conditions give rise to arising.
What relevance does this have to arising and ceasing?
Therefore, one should know that the phenomenon of cessation ceases spontaneously.
Second, by inferring from the fruits currently being experienced, one knows the past causes that are not presently perceived.

The meaning of this objection is as follows: If it were the case that those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise solely with that Īśvara as their condition, then they should have existed primordially together with that Īśvara; why, then, would they need to be produced anew?
If Īśvara were primordially existent,
then at the very time he exists, all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) would also exist;
since all conditioned phenomena would thus be simultaneous with Īśvara, [they would lack a cause].
Therefore, one should know that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are likewise inherently existent.
If they were inherently existent, they would be eternally abiding and should not be called "conditioned phenomena.
This is because, according to that [opponent's] doctrine, conditioned phenomena are not inherently existent.
Having seen this difficulty,
he then further established that Īśvara exists by nature from the beginning.
Since all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise subsequently, the subsequent treatise states: "If one says that Īśvara and so forth exist prior [to them].
The Master [Vasubandhu] perceived this shift in their position.
He then further pursues the difficulty, saying:
"If conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise only after volition (*svatantra*),
then these phenomena do not arise solely through volition, as they must also depend on other distinct conditions."
Therefore, the subsequent treatise states: "Thus, these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) do not arise solely with Īśvara as their condition.

If Īśvara were used as their condition, then since Īśvara exists at all times and conditioned phenomena exist [at those times], they should both be inherently existent (*sahaja*) from the very beginning."
If subsequent formations were to arise only later,
then those subsequent formations would only emerge due to the power of aspiration; thus,
if formations take aspiration as their cause, [they would not arise spontaneously].
For what reason is it argued that Īśvara alone is the cause?

Therefore, the subsequent treatise states: "If one says that Īśvara acts according to his own desires, such as through effort (*prayatna*) or prayer (*prārthanā*)," since this already concedes that desire is the cause.
This must further be examined and refuted;
therefore, the subsequent treatise asks: "If that is so, does this desire have a cause? and so forth.
This posits the hypothetical case where desire has a cause, namely, that it takes Īśvara as its cause.
Since mastery is inherently existent, desire should also be inherently existent;
for when there is mastery, desire exists as well. This is refuted by the same arguments previously applied to the conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
Therefore, the subsequent treatise states: "If one says there is a cause, it must be Īśvara and so forth.
Having already refuted the desire to take Īśvara as the cause, there may subsequently be other causes that do not take Īśvara as their cause.
If that is so, and desire possesses a cause,
then just as the aforementioned formations (*saṃskāra*) previously had the distinct function of desire, effort, and aspiration as their causes,
it is now stated that they further have as their cause a distinct factor other than the sovereign (*īśvara*), namely desire, effort, and aspiration.
Thus, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise from distinct causes;
why then needlessly and falsely imagine a useless *Īśvara*?
Therefore, the treatise next states: "If one says that this desire has yet another cause, etc."
The phrase "Thus, briefly, by means of the power of these three types of predominant mental attention (*adhipati-manasikāra*)...
and so forth, concludes the discussion on the mental attention of the three measures (*pramāṇa*).
Next, the specific modes of separation (*viyoga-prakāra*) are explained.
First, the preceding section is restated to introduce the subsequent one;
next, it is explained;
finally, it is concluded.
Regarding the phrase "the five modes of practice previously cited" mentioned earlier:
the beginning of the fascicle states that among the four modes of practice under the Truth of Suffering,
one enters into the realization of impermanence through the first five of those five modes.
Among these five modes of activity, the first is the mode of transformation (*vipariṇāma-gati*).
This refers to the eight kinds of causal conditions, the fifteen kinds, the sixteen kinds, and so forth, of transformation previously explained.
The second is the mode of disintegration (*vināśa-gati*).
This refers precisely to what was previously explained regarding the inference that there is momentary arising and ceasing, and so forth.
Thus, it is said that the two modes of observation have already been analyzed.
Now, as for the third, why does one again observe the nature of impermanence by means of the mode of separation?
In the commentary,
it says: "That which is not desired" refers to an enemy.
Regarding "and shared property" and so forth: it refers to common property.
Alternatively, it refers to that which is lost or destroyed through the application of misconduct.
To fail to act when one ought to is called "regret" (kaukṛtya).
Regarding the phrase "within the practice of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā)," it refers to all that is subject to transformation, impermanence, and so forth.
The meaning here is as follows: when one is currently experiencing a pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) and correctly receiving pleasure, it has not yet undergone transformation or impermanence;
[this is stated] by way of the three types of impermanent modes (*anityākāra*), beginning with transformation (*vipariṇāma*).
One contemplates that present pleasant feelings will necessarily be impermanent in the future;
thus one penetrates that such pleasant feelings will certainly be impermanent in the future.
Therefore, it is called "contemplating impermanence by means of the impermanence of the dharma-nature" because it causes one to bring [the present] into accord with these three types of impermanence;
that is to say, when contemplating impermanence, one brings the present phenomena into accord with these three types of impermanence.
This is called the impermanence of conjunction.
It means that the aforementioned pleasant sensations flow into these three types of impermanence within the present life.
Second, it clarifies the entry into the practice of suffering through the three modes of existence.

Thus, regarding the statement "by means of the reasoning of proof and the predominance of cultivation, one arrives at the entry into ascetic practice," this concludes the preceding section and introduces the subsequent one; that is to say,
it refers to the authoritative scripture (āptāgama) and direct perception (pratyakṣa) with inference (anumāna) as explained above.
These three constitute the principles of proof (*upapatti-sādhana*) herein.

Regarding the phrase "and because of the predominance of cultivation," this refers to the principle of relying on the authoritative teaching (*āptāgama*), as stated immediately below: "By the power of the attention characterized by the predominance of pure faith in one who practices according to the teaching."
Whether by the predominant power of direct perception,
or by the predominant power of such inference, and so forth—
it is because of the predominance of these and of cultivation therein.
He individually contemplates each [topic], beginning with "the authoritative scripture" (*āptāgama*) and so forth;
this mental attention (*manasikāra*) is itself the cultivation of increase (*vṛddhi-bhāvanā*).
Next, the explanation follows.
The subsequent section provides a summary. This explains the second mode, the "unpleasant course" (*apriya-gati*), which was previously analyzed.
The first mode, the "course bound by fetters" (*saṃyojana-bandhana-gati*), is explained separately because its order differs from that in the enumeration of names.
Third, the explanation of the practice of insecurity (*anairyāṇika-carita*).

At the beginning, one reflects as follows: "All such conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent," and so forth, up to: "In this way, through the practice of the unattractive (*aśubha*), one enters into the practice of suffering (*duḥkha*)," and so on.
Master Ji’s commentary explains:
According to the following passage,
[it refers to] those formations that are conducive to painful feeling, as well as within painful feeling itself.
One enters into the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) by way of the aspect of the unlovely;
that is, one enters into the suffering of suffering within these three [aspects] by means of this very aspect.
Within this aspect of the unlovely, the preceding seven types of suffering are subsumed.
All seven types of suffering are the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
According to the *Abhidharmapitaka* and other texts, among these seven sufferings, the first five are the suffering of suffering,
while the following two are the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).
Regarding that which contradicts this text,
it is first explained as follows: among the seven types of suffering associated with the aspect of the unlovely (*an-iṣṭa-gati*),
the first five are the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).

Now, because these three modes of conduct—the unlovely, the bound, and the insecure—are subsumed under the three types of suffering respectively, they are thus subsumed. Within the category of the unlovely, although there are two types of suffering, both are included within the mode of suffering as suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
Because the few arise from the many, the two types of suffering constitute the five types of suffering.
Furthermore, because these [seven] give rise to the feeling of suffering in accordance with their nature,
all seven are indeed the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).

Why is this? Because, within the sequence of the second clarification regarding the practice of fetters and bonds, one enters into the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*) by means of those fetters and bonds;
that is, from the fetters such as poverty and craving, there further arises greed, attachment, and so forth.

The teaching that birth, old age, sickness, death, and so forth constitute the great mass of suffering means that those [factors] which give rise to pleasant feelings are suffering through change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*). Therefore,
it is known that those [factors] which give rise to painful feelings are suffering through suffering itself (*duḥkhaduḥkha*).
Because the arising of equanimity from feelings that are neither painful nor pleasant constitutes the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Regarding the differences between the preceding and following sections of this treatise on entering the three types of suffering,
they should be understood by seeking their essential nature and characteristics according to the requirements of the context.
Furthermore, regarding the distinctions in the categories of inclusion (*saṃgraha-artha-mukha*):
since that treatise subsumes the eight sufferings under the three types of suffering (*tri-duḥkhatā*), one knows that five [of the eight] are the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
Since this treatise subsumes the eight sufferings under the three modes of activity (*tri-ākāra*), the mode of being unlovely (*aniṣṭa-ākāra*) constitutes the first seven modes of activity.
Now, because suffering encompasses the three modes of activity (*saṃskāra*), the mode of activity that is unlovely is encompassed by the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*);

it is not that the seven types of suffering encompassed by the mode of activity that is unlovely are themselves designated as the suffering of suffering by virtue of being encompassed by the suffering of suffering.
Therefore, there is no contradiction;
they differ in their categorization of meanings.
As for the statement "with outflows and with grasping":
Duke Jing said:
"Leakage is affliction;
grasping is nothing but craving."
Apart from the Path that leads to cessation, all other forms of suffering and its origin are capable of producing outflows (*āsrava*).
Furthermore, because they arise from conditions, they are called "with outflows" (*sāsrava*);
and because they arise from grasping and further produce grasping through rebirth, they are called "with grasping" (*sopādāna*).
Regarding the aggregates that are neither painful nor pleasant,
one enters into the practice of suffering by way of their mode of being non-peaceful; this refers generally to the essential nature of the formations (*saṃskāra*).
This refers to all contaminated aggregates that accord with the three types of sensation.
In this text, in order to distinguish them from those aggregates that accord with the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*),
it speaks only of the contaminated aggregates that accord with neither-suffering-nor-pleasure as being the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
In this context, the ālayavijñāna is described as being "conducive to the aggregate of equanimity" because it is accompanied by the seeds of suffering and pleasure.
However, the text states that all aggregates conducive to neither-suffering-nor-pleasure are accompanied by the seeds of both suffering and pleasure.
It does not refer exclusively to that ālayavijñāna;
therefore, one should know that this is established as the ālayavijñāna based on its final [state].
For this reason, it is explained generally as being accompanied by the seeds of suffering and pleasure within all the aggregates (skandhas).
Thus, regarding the statement that all formations (*saṃskāra*) up to all sensations (*vedanā*) are suffering:
this clarifies the meaning of the three types of craving being suffering as taught in the *Saṃyuktāgama*.
Third, it clarifies the practice of non-apprehension as the entry into the practice of emptiness.
Jing says: "One contemplates that the continuity of the mind is free from a second dharma, such that there is only this mind."
Because there is no self apart from the mind, it is called "emptiness.
Because there is no self within the aggregates, it is called "selflessness.
The fourth [section] clarifies the practice of non-mastery as entering into the mode of selflessness.
Master Ji said:
"What is the difference between the two practices of emptiness and non-self?
Emptiness is definitively concerned with the essence."
The concentration on non-self is applied precisely for this purpose:
that which is reckoned as having an essence is called "existence," and emptiness is used to dispel it.
To grasp at that which has utility and name it as "self" is to be countered by the absence of self (*anātman*).
This is the second explanation within the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
There are three successive expositions.
In the first exposition, the causes, accumulations, arisings, and conditions are explained.

Regarding the statement, "It is understood that craving is called the cause because it can draw forth suffering": this means that craving is designated as the cause because it is known to be capable of inducing the arising of suffering.
Jingyun says:
"Because craving necessarily draws forth suffering, craving is generally described as the cause of suffering.
Jiji says: [as follows].
Furthermore, for example, when one encounters a present object conducive to pleasant feeling and gives rise to craving toward it,
one should know that this immediately perfumes [the mind] to form the seeds of craving and so forth.
At the time these seeds are formed, they further cause the seeds of future birth and so forth to increase therein.
This craving is called the "cause" (*hetu*) because it is capable of drawing forth and producing the seeds of birth and so forth;
once suffering has been drawn forth, it further gathers and brings it into existence, and for this reason it is called "origination" (*samudaya*). Thus says Jing.
Craving, having already drawn forth suffering, further gathers karma that causes future suffering to arise; this is called "origination" (*samudaya*).

Jiqi states: "That is to say, the aforementioned craving moistens the constituent of formations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth, thereby constituting the capacity for origination (*samudaya*) that produces future results."
This craving is called "accumulation" (samudaya) because it can accumulate the conditions for others;
since it causes suffering to arise once it has been produced, it is said to be "origination" (samudaya). Jing says:
Once that karma has been accumulated and the birth of suffering has occurred, it now causes suffering to arise;
this is what is meant by saying that craving "arises. Ji says:
Once craving has already perfumed the seeds, it can cause the seeds of suffering to produce the actual manifestation (*samudācāra*) of birth and other forms of suffering.
Because craving can cause the seeds of birth and so forth to arise as actual manifestations, it is called "arising" (*utthāna*).
Regarding the statement that it is called a "condition" (*pratyaya*) because it can grasp the seeds of future suffering and sequentially attract and induce the accumulation of suffering: Jing says,
"This craving (*tṛṣṇā*) does not merely lead to the manifestation of present suffering and the arising of future suffering."
Furthermore, it is called a condition because it can attract and cause the seeds of future suffering, such as consciousness and so forth, to increase. Ji says:
"Since craving itself is able to grasp, perfume, and increase the seeds of future suffering..."
That which causes the successive arising of future suffering, such as birth and so forth—the origin of all suffering—is designated as "condition.
This first sequence is roughly consistent with the sixth fascicle of the *Abhidharma-piṭaka*.
Examine this further.
Moreover, there is a distinction between the general and the specific.

Regarding the meaning of these categories: the fact that all forms of craving can crave for a future self-identity is termed "the drawing forth of suffering" (*ākarṣaṇa-duḥkha*); this is the general definition.
The remaining three are distinct.

Having already projected suffering, craving causes the fruits of the three realms and five destinies to manifest in the present and accumulate as future results; therefore, it is called "origination" (*samudaya*).

Having already projected the karma for the five destinies, craving subsequently causes the birth of a single individual within those destinies and so forth to manifest in the present; therefore, it is called "birth" (*jāti*).

Once the rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*) of a single person in a particular realm of existence has manifested, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) causes the various stages within that person’s life—such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth—to arise in succession and manifest; this is called "condition" (*pratyaya*).
These three [stages] arise sequentially and individually.
Consulting the sixth fascicle, it is the same as this.
The meaning of the second "furthermore" (punar-apara) is that the link of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) serves as the cause for the link of grasping (*upādāna*).
The limb of craving (*tṛṣṇā-aṅga*), in relation to the limb of existence (*bhava-aṅga*), serves as the cause of origination (*samudaya*) because it is capable of accumulating all karmas;
that is, it causes the limb of birth (*jāti-aṅga*) to manifest, which is termed "arising" (*utthāna*).
Furthermore, the limb of craving is able to bring about the manifestation of the limbs of aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa-aṅga*), which is termed the "remote condition" (*dūre-pratyaya*).
Section Two on Understanding: Furthermore, it is said that among the twelve links, craving is called a "cause" because it is known to be the cause of grasping.
This craving is not only the cause of grasping, but is also capable of summoning and gathering the existence (bhava) produced by grasping.
Fearing that [the definition] might overextend to the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), it now specifies "existence that has grasping as its cause.
Therefore, it says: "precisely because it is existence that has grasping as its cause.
Furthermore, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is able to give rise to the future branch of birth (*jāti*).
The birth-link arises from the existence-link;
since existence is cited as the cause of birth,
it is said that existence is the primary factor.
Because it gives rise to craving in the future and can further trigger old age, sickness, death, and so forth, it is called a "condition" (*pratyaya*).
By citing birth as the condition, the intended meaning is that one regards the resulting old age, sickness, death, and so forth as the objects conditioned by it.
Regarding the third "furthermore," Jing says:
"This refers to correctly understanding that which serves as the cause for future existence."

Regarding the attention that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*): he correctly understands that the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) such as craving (*tṛṣṇā*) based upon the ālayavijñāna are the cause of future existence (*punarbhava*).

Furthermore, he correctly understands that the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) produced by those [latent tendencies] are, according to their respective natures, the conditions for the origination of the accumulation [of suffering].
This provides a general explanation that the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) arising from the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) constitute the condition for the origination of suffering.
Below follows a specific explanation:
craving for future existence (*punarbhava-tṛṣṇā*) brings about the gathering of future existence; thus, it is called "origination" (*samudaya*).
Thereafter, craving for existence further gives rise to craving that is accompanied by joy and lust regarding one's own present body; therefore, it is called "arising.
Furthermore, this craving accompanied by joy and lust serves as the condition for various kinds of requisites and the respective craving for them; thus, it is called the "condition."
Master Ji says:
The meaning of the third "furthermore" (punar) is as follows:

one understands that the seeds of all afflictions, which are attached to the foundational consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as their support, along with the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of craving and so forth, are called the "cause" because they are the productive cause for future existence in a subsequent life.
To know that the seed of craving has the capacity to produce future fruit is termed "knowing the cause.
This single type of seed subsequently manifests as the three types of craving;
because this craving further summons and gathers future existence (*punarbhava*), it is termed "origination" (*samudaya*).
Thereafter, with craving as a condition, one is further able to give rise to craving that proceeds together with joy and lust toward present objects; this is called "arising.
With this very craving that proceeds together [with joy and lust] as a condition, one gives rise to craving for various joys and pleasures toward future objects; this is called "conditioning."
Among these four types of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), the present craving that clings to one's own self is not mentioned.
Furthermore, this [present craving] is itself the first of the four cravings, which is designated simply as "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*).
This craving is craving in its general sense;
its specific characteristics are difficult to discern.
Now, by using the term "seed," it is indicated that its actual nature extends to both the latent state and active manifestation.
Although the treatise speaks of "afflictions in general," its intent is to refer specifically to craving (*tṛṣṇā*),
because this craving is capable of projecting future results.
The other three [afflictions] constitute the three types of craving.
It is said that this craving for future existence further gives rise to craving accompanied by joy and greed;
this craving accompanied by joy and greed arises in relation to present objects.
Both types of craving take the future self as their object, because they both crave the body of a future existence.
Because it can also generate craving toward present objects, it is called "concomitant craving" (*sahagata-tṛṣṇā*).
With craving for future existence (*punarbhava-tṛṣṇā*) as its cause,
and because craving arises in connection with excellent present objects, one also gives rise to various forms of "liking and craving" (*nandī-rāga*) toward excellent future objects.
Therefore, those various forms of craving and delight also have concurrent craving as their condition.
Regarding the third explanation, among the four aspects of the Truth of Cessation:
the absence of remainder of the Truth of Origination is called "cessation," and the absence of remainder of the Truth of Suffering is called "tranquility."
These are precisely the two aforementioned types.
The first is called "sublime" because it is most excellent and unsurpassed;
these are precisely the two aforementioned types.
That which is eternally abiding and characterized by renunciation is called "detachment" (*niḥsaraṇa*). Regarding the fourth [truth], the path:
among its four aspects, it is called the "path" (*mārga*) because it functions as a road that enables the seeking of access toward the object of knowledge, namely cessation (*nirodha*).
Because the path leads to the sought-after Dharma,
and that which is sought encompasses both the false and the real,
this sought-after reality— which is not false— is called "Suchness" (tathatā).
Because it eliminates falsehood,
it is not only able to seek the truth within the Truth of Cessation,
but is also able to know all four truths as they truly are through their respective gates; this capacity to accord with and proceed along them is called "practice" (*caryā*).
Because it traverses the Four Noble Truths.
What is the purpose of this practice that traverses the Four Noble Truths?
It is called "exit" (*niḥsaraṇa*) because it has the sense of being able to emerge from birth-and-death and proceed resolutely toward Nirvāṇa.
Because it emerges from all weariness and toil.
Second, regarding the clarification of the contemplation of the Four Truths of the upper realms:
first, the preceding section is concluded and the subsequent section is introduced.
Second, the correct explanation:
regarding the passage "all that exists, up to and including all having such a nature," Jing says:
This clarifies the essence of the conditioned, contaminated *duḥkha-satya* within the two upper realms.
It pervades all places of birth in the upper realms;
the aggregate of craving and so forth pervades the seeds of the five sense-gates.
Throughout the three periods of time, there are always such phenomena of the origin of suffering;
all follow this principle of the truth of origination (samudaya-satya) and all possess the nature of the truth of suffering (duḥkha-satya).
The lower section clarifies that the cessation and path of the upper realms can likewise be known.
Master Ji states:
"The intention here is to contemplate the principle of the Four Noble Truths."

Having perceived that the aggregates seen within this realm are impermanent and so forth, one is able to use reasoning to infer and examine all the aggregates that are not currently visible in other dissimilar realms.
This refers to all conditioned and out-flowing phenomena belonging to other realms and so forth, which pertain to the three realms and their locations,
and which are planted within all aggregates throughout all times of the three periods.
All possess such a collection of factors capable of producing effects:
the truth of suffering, consisting of the difficult-to-reconcile conditions of birth, aging, and so forth.

All those who follow this principle of suffering and impermanence possess the nature of a common cause for arising through the accumulation of karma and afflictions; this is the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya).
If their nature, conduct, and existence are subject to cessation, and there is the peace and bliss of nirvāṇa, this is the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya).
That path which is capable of severing all afflictions and providing ultimate deliverance from birth and death is the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
The intent of this passage is to exhort the practitioner to use what is currently perceived here as an analogy for the aggregates and so forth in other realms that are not currently perceived.
From here below is the third section, which summarizes that the three types of wisdom are the basis for producing the seeds of dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Jing says: "The three preceding expedient means explained above..."
Relying on the preparatory concentration (anāgamya-samādhi),
one cultivates the attention that marks the signs of arising and observes the truths from both above and below.
It is able to immediately perfume and activate the seeds of the dharma-knowledge and subsequent-knowledge within the innate相见道 (xiàngjiàn dào), causing them to increase;
this is called taking the [mental] factors and the seeds as its locus. Tái says:
From the perspective of the contemplations on the dharmas and subsequent knowledge prior to the path of seeing,
one looks forward to the true contemplations on the dharmas and subsequent knowledge after the path as the seeds and basis;
this is identical to the seeds of liberation from the mind-free meditative concentration.
Master Ji says:

The meaning here is that because one performs these practices of the Four Truths through the five meditative cessations (*pañca-sthāpana*) and the general and specific applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*),
this constitutes the locus for the seeds of the subsequent untainted subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).

First, because that which is with outflows (sāsrava) serves as a condition capable of inducing the outflow-free (anāsrava), it is called the "basis for seeds," which carries the meaning of being newly perfumed (navasaṃskṛta).
Second, even at the time of the five preliminary practices (pañca-vasthāna), one is likewise able to perfume and increase the beginningless outflow-free seeds.
This type of dwelling is also included within the stage of the "attention that discerns characteristics" (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*) among the five stages of cessation;
because it is capable of producing the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) of the initial path of seeing,
it is called the basis for the seeds of dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge.
The following clarifies the stages and levels.

That is to say, the sixteen types of mental engagement (manasikāra) characterized by the aspects explained above still involve the hearing and reflection of the desire realm, as well as their intermingling.
This is situated within the five cessations and the general and specific applications of mindfulness;

it is the first section, which concludes the preceding [discussion] and provides a brief thematic heading, occurring within the second [section], the mental attention of resolution (*adhimukti-manasikāra*).
The second part is the detailed explanation.

Within the former [section], it means that following the attention consisting of the discernment of characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedanamanaskāra*), one subsequently gives rise to the attention consisting of resolute belief (*adhimuktimanaskāra*).
Furthermore, one engenders resolute belief regarding the nature of things as they are (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) within the various phenomena of the Four Truths.

The mental application of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*) refers to the generation of resolute conviction regarding the equality of the four truths as the single nature of true suchness (*tathatā*) and the nature of things as they are (*yathāvadbhāvatā*);
its stage is situated within the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), beginning with "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).
Within the extensive explanation,
the analysis of the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśalamūla*) is divided into four sections.
The first explains the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).
The text is divided into two parts.
The first explains the characteristics of mental attention (*manasikāra*) cultivated in relation to the "extent of existence" (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) of the truths.
The second begins with: "In this way, the practitioner of yoga who has diligently practiced... and so forth.
This clarifies that the realization of the four truths (*catur-āryasatya-abhisamaya*) takes the "nature as it is" (*yathāvadbhāva*) as its object.

Regarding the statement that such mental attention (*manasikāra*) previously described takes only the objects of the truths as its domain and remains exclusively in meditative concentration (*samāhita*), Kīrti says:

Regarding this attention (*manasikāra*), in the section concerning the abandonment of the conceit of self (*asmimāna*), the text states that "coarse-grade conceit of self arises intermittently and continuously.
This attention of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*) arises intermittently and continuously because it is [interrupted] by the conceit of self.
Why is it said that [the mind] is "always in meditative concentration"?
Is this not contradictory?
The meaning is as follows:
When the mental attention characterized by clear comprehension (*pariśuddha-nimitta-manasikāra*) takes a single object with a wholesome mind,
because it is interspersed with hearing and reflection while taking the same object,
the arising of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) is exclusively wholesome.
When perceiving each individual object, one is not interspersed with hearing or reflection, but remains consistently in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

To distinguish this from the "characteristic-perceiving" (*lakṣaṇa-prativedha*) stage, the term "consistently" (*ekānta*) is used. This is stated according to the perspective of being for the most part in a virtuous state of mind during a single contemplation.
It is not that they do not emerge from meditative absorption to give rise to the conceit of "I" (asmimāna) or to regress and produce other afflictions;
rather, it is because [the author] does not wish to clarify the suppression of the conceit of "I," but intends to discuss the actual attainment of the conceit of "I."
Therefore, it is said that there is an uninterrupted transition between them.
Now, because the characteristic of discernment (*lakṣaṇapraveśa*) is distinguished by resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), it persists for a long duration within meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*).

This is not like the characteristic of discernment [in the stage of] hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī*), which cannot enter meditative observation for a long duration due to being interrupted by those [stages].
The term "exclusively" (ekānta) does not imply contradiction;
it means that such phenomena as the flow of birth and death are boundless and so forth.
This section fully elucidates the boundlessness of the Four Noble Truths;
the meaning of the text may be understood accordingly. Tai says:
All phenomena of birth and death are without support and without acquisition; they cannot be taken as a basis.
One should give rise to practice that is without support, being free from all expectations and seeing only suffering and affliction.
Therefore, one gives rise to the practice of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). Jing said:
"Although one may weary of suffering and its accumulation (*duḥkha-samudaya*) and rejoice in the bliss of nirvana (*nirvāṇa*)."
Nevertheless, they are still unable to enter with a deep resolve.
Why is this? Because they still possess a coarse form of the conceit "I am," which acts as an obstacle to clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
Regarding "the mental engagement of following entry (*anupraviṣṭa-manasikāra*) that operates without interval":
when one contemplates the flow of saṃsāra and so forth, the mind carries a sense of "I," which is called *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am").

This state of carrying the notion of "I" is termed coarse *asmimāna*. The mental engagement of following entry and the mental engagement of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣika-manasikāra*)—the mind contemplating the Four Noble Truths—operate in immediate succession with one another.
By reflecting in this way, up to the point of thinking "these various phenomena are mine," one eliminates the coarse forms of the conceit of "I.
Once he has understood that such conceit is an obstacle, he applies himself with focused attention, diligence, and uninterrupted continuity.
Fearing that the conceit of "I" might arise again as an obstacle,
he applies himself with diligence and uninterrupted effort to subdue the objects of knowledge and enter into nirvāṇa;
this continues until the final moment of mind arises.
Observe whether the preceding mind is deviant or correct,
guarding it with single-minded diligence and without interruption,
so that no room is left for the arising of conceit.
Tai said: "Because one cannot initiate entry,
one should simply initiate the mental application of effortless cultivation."
Having thus understood the obstacle of the conceit of "I," he is able to swiftly and with dedicated,
uninterrupted effort abandon the previously cultivated state of effortless mental engagement.
In this way, until finally, by taking the subsequent contemplative mind as the object of the preceding contemplative mind, he becomes free from the signs of the focal object.
Master Ki says:
"As for the passage 'Since he has already understood... up to entering the mental attention' and so forth, this 'conforming mental attention' is none other than the aforementioned 'I-conceit'."
Because one is able to enter [the truth] by means of this internal self in accordance with the Dharma, it is called "attention of following entry" (*anupraveśamanasikāra*).
Regarding "attention of entering" (*avatārāmanasikāra*):
it refers to having already long wandered through birth and death and being destined to wander there once again.
Even up to the point where signlessness is truly signless, that which arises by taking external objects as its object is called "the attention of entry.
Following this attention, the practitioner observes the Noble Truths with focused diligence and uninterrupted continuity.
Once this observing mind has ceased, there subsequently arises a continuous flow of the skillful means of observation without interval;
the preceding observing mind subsides and the subsequent observing mind arises.
Thereafter, the subsequent mind takes the preceding mind as its object with unflagging and exclusive concentration.
For this reason, it is impossible for any coarse form of *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am") to arise;
such is the meaning of the passage.
From here below is the second section, which clarifies the contemplation of the four truths based on the nature of things as they are (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*).
In this way, the practitioner contemplates that the continuum of the mind arises anew at every moment in a state of mutual differentiation, sometimes increasing and sometimes decreasing.
Master Ji said:
"When a practitioner performs meditative contemplation, if each successive moment increases in excellence, it is called 'increasing' (or *vṛddhi*).
If it does not decrease from that increasing excellence, it is called 'not decreasing' (*avṛddhi*)."
Since there is a sudden arising for a moment followed by increase, decrease, and transformation throughout the preceding and succeeding states, it is clearly known to be impermanent.
Furthermore, as this very observation of the mind enters into the appropriated aggregates (upādānaskandha), it is clearly known to be suffering.

There is no such thing as a truly real dharma; rather, it is simply that dharmas are suffering. This is called the contemplation of emptiness. The nature of the mind is suffering, for the dharma that is falsely grasped is itself suffering.
This is because one contemplates the absence of a second dharma.
The meaning here is that "impermanence" refers to the fact that what is falsely imagined as real dharmas is empty;
"selflessness" refers to the absence of sovereign agency.
This is the intended sense.
In calculation, one takes the Truth of the Path as its object, regarding it as impermanent and so forth;

this is because, from the perspective of the mind that resembles [actual] contemplation, it is the Truth of the Path. However, according to the actual mind of contemplation, it is the Truth of Suffering.
Because it is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*),
this is now explained in terms of its conformity to the supramundane meaning;
furthermore, because within this stage there is the sense of being untainted (*anāsrava*).
It is taught as the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
If one were to rely on this [conventional] meaning, it would also take the Truth of the Path as its object through aspects such as impermanence;
however, since we are now relying on the ultimate meaning (*bhūtārtha*), it is the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
Jingyun: To know that there is only mind and no second self or dharmas is called emptiness.
One who correctly awakens to and enters the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path draws closer to the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*).
The gradual increase in clarity of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) is called "correct entry";
it is not the case that direct realization (*abhisamaya*) itself is termed "entry.
As contemplative practice gradually increases, one becomes free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Therefore, it is said that when the subject that perceives and the object perceived are equal and identical, right knowledge arises.
Next, the stages of *mūrdhan* (Summit) and *kṣānti* (Patience) are explained. Jing says:
Those four roots of goodness that peacefully accept the principle of the Truths are all termed "patience" (kṣānti).
However, they are established as "Heat," "Summit," and "Patience" based on three grades. Tái says:
Because one trains in the contemplation of the emptiness of persons and non-self,
and because one also seals the principle of truth with equanimity and equality,
these are both termed "patience" (kṣānti).
Regarding the fourth explanation, concerning the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*):
since he has already extensively practiced up to the point of abiding in a mind that is free from applied effort and non-conceptualization,
he has cultivated this repeatedly from the preceding stages.
Therefore, having abandoned preparatory effort (*prayoga*), one abides in non-conceptual mind (*nirvikalpa-citta*).
Regarding the statement that "this mind appears to cease but does not actually cease; it appears to lack an object (*ālambana*) but does not lack an object," Ke says:
Non-conceptual wisdom, being quiescent and subtle, is termed "cessation.
Since this [state] resembles that [wisdom] but is not actually that wisdom itself,
it is called "resembling cessation."
Furthermore, non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna) is called "cessation" because it extinguishes the conceptualizing mind;
now, this [state] resembles that, and is thus called "resembling cessation.
Moreover, the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) is also termed "cessation."
Because the mind is subtle, it resembles that meditative absorption of cessation;
thus it is called "resembling cessation.
Non-conceptual wisdom has no objective referent (ālambana) consisting of mental images.
Now, this signless [state] resembles that [object],
yet there is an image; therefore,
it is said to resemble that which lacks an objective referent (*ālambana*).
Furthermore, because these objects are present before one, it is not the case that there is no object of cognition (*ālambana*).
Although the mind is subtle and appears as if without an object, it is not without an object.
Moreover, non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is free from conceptualization, detached from all signs (*nimitta*), and detached from all afflictions (*kleśa*).
Now, because this resembles that, although it is said to resemble detachment, it is not true detachment. Jing says:

The roots of goodness such as "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth are, according to their respective degrees, quiescent and resemble the true untainted mind of detachment;
however, their essence is tainted (*sāsrava*) and not [itself] detachment. Tai says:
