This refers to the internal mental attention directed toward the principles of the Truths at the very last moment of the mind abiding in tranquility within the four roots of goodness; this is called the "Supreme Mundane Dharma.
Regarding this, there are two interpretations.
One interpretation states:
This passage proves that the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgradharma) takes all four truths as its object and performs the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*).
Since the treatise refers to "the principle of all noble truths," we know it does not concern only a single truth.
This text follows the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* in stating that the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) also takes the four truths as its object,
differing from the minor treatises which hold it takes only the truth of suffering as its object.
Second, it says:
The Supreme Mundane Dharma takes only one Truth as its object, as stated in the *Abhidharmakośa*.
In this present text, the characteristics are presented by taking both the general and the specific;
that is to say, it refers to the internal mental attention directed toward any one of the principles of the Noble Truths previously examined during the stages of Heat and so forth.
However, regarding the statement in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* that one contemplates the Four Truths,
Master Huiyuan explained that there are two kinds of contemplation of the truths:
first, that which is acquired through cultivation and arises in the present.
Second, there is the cultivation through attainment (*pratilambhabhāvanā*) of what is to be accomplished in the future.
Although the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) cultivated in the present contemplate only one Truth and one aspect,
they increase the clarity of the future images regarding the four truths in their entirety.
Now, regarding the name "attaining cultivation," it refers to taking the four truths as its object.
In explaining that sutra, we likewise employ the general to include the specific;
for although the four truths are mentioned collectively, the intent is actually to take the truth of suffering.

Regarding the third explanation, within the context of "the mental attention of seclusion," concerning the phrase "from immediately after this until the arising of the knowledge of direct perception" and so forth,
Jing says:
Immediately following this Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*),
one gives rise to internal mental attention (*manasikāra*) regarding the principles of the Noble Truths previously contemplated during the stage prior to the Supreme Mundane Dharma.
Immediately upon that mental attention, one contemplates the various truths in the same sequence as they were previously observed.
If the Four Truths of the desire realm are directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*),
those of the two higher realms are termed "not directly perceived.
Just as immediately following the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), there arises the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), which is a non-conceptual, certain, and directly perceiving wisdom.
Because this wisdom arises, all the heavy residues (*dausthulya*) of the delusions of view within the three realms are forever severed.
Tai says: "Immediately following this true path of vision (*darśanamārga*)."
Subsequently, within the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*), one again contemplates the various Truths previously explained.
As the aforementioned treatise states, "When supramundane mind arises, that is true vision (*bhūta-darśana*)," it elaborately sets forth three meanings.
Regarding the statement that since there are already dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) among the preliminary preparations for the path of insight (darśana-mārga),
one should know that they likewise exist within the true contemplation;
however, although dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge are of many kinds.
The meaning of this passage is that one contemplates desire as "dharmas" and contemplates the higher realms as "categories. Furthermore,
it is explained as follows:
Since the true path of vision (*darśanamārga*) consists of a single moment of consciousness, the cognitions of the four truths are distinguished according to their respective modes of application;
hence it is said, "in succession.
Those of dull faculties, however, contemplate the four truths individually.
Therefore, it is said "in sequence.
The former interpretation is superior. Ki says:
Immediately following the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) of the previous life,

one now gives rise to internal mental attention (*adhyātma-manasikāra*) within the true path of vision (*darśanamārga*), based upon the principles of the Noble Truths as they were previously contemplated during that supreme mundane dharma.
Immediately following this mental attention (*manasikāra*) of the true path of seeing,

within the path of seeing characterized by images (*sākāra-darśanamārga*), one likewise directly perceives those truths that were previously observed during the first moment of the stage of "Dharma" (*dharmajñāna*).
Furthermore, regarding the noble truths that are not directly perceived, such as those in different realms or dimensions,
there exists an untainted, non-conceptual certainty concerning their sequence— such as suffering, its origin, and so forth.
Doubt and wisdom arise spontaneously from within oneself rather than being induced by others;
they are produced through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
and are not like the conceptual doubt that arises prior to the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) through inference and estimation.
This is the intended meaning here.
Furthermore, the term "immediately following" (*anantara*) in the phrase "immediately following the World-First Dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma-anantara*) refers to this very sequence.
Now, the intention is to explain the True Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), which is difficult to understand.
Having finished explaining the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
we now turn back to explain its immediate precursor, the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).
This will now establish what was previously mentioned.

This refers to the time when one gives rise to internal mental attention (*manasikāra*) toward the principles of the Noble Truths previously contemplated; this is precisely at the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).

Immediately following this mental attention, with respect to the truths contemplated in their prior sequence, there arises within the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*)—whether they be presently perceived or not—a definitive knowledge and a knowledge of direct perception.
This is also the intended meaning here.
Since this treatise concerns their permanent abandonment, it refers to those who have already detached from the craving of the desire realm and will never again return to be born in this world.
In this context, it refers to one who has previously used the worldly path to suppress and abandon the desires of the desire realm;
when they now enter the path of seeing, they achieve the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
This is precisely what is meant by a person who "leaps over" to become a non-returner.
For now, we shall base our discussion on the non-returner who has detached from the desire realm,
without considering those who have previously detached from up to the sphere of nothingness. Furthermore,
the characteristics of one who is detached from desire through mundane means were not explained in the preceding fascicle.
Their deportment is tranquil and their speech is grave and earnest, free from agitation and the like;
as this now resembles that, it is said: "One should know they are no different," and so forth.
Furthermore, although they are similar, there is a slight distinction:
the Non-returner (anāgāmin) is not reborn in the desire realm,
but attains parinirvāṇa right there.
This is not the case for those in the world who have abandoned desire;
therefore, there is a distinction.

Because the knowing wisdom and the known object are conjoined without discord and are directly perceived before one, it is called "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*); this should be understood to apply likewise to the *brāhmaṇas* and others.
When entering the path of seeing and realizing suchness,
the object— suchness— is signless;
therefore, the wisdom [that realizes it] is also signless.
Second, there is the harmony of signlessness:
the subject that perceives and the object perceived are free from the discordance of signs;
one observes this directly before oneself.
Therefore, it is called "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*). To explain the meaning of the term "clear realization":
it is like when a Kṣatriya meets with another Kṣatriya in one place; there is no discord between their intentions.
Because they share the same spiritual lineage (*gotra*), they constitute a single class;
this is also termed "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*).
Brahmins and others should know that it is likewise so.
Regarding the phrase "this also accomplishes numerous characteristics and so forth":
it clarifies that for one who enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there are twelve characteristics.
First, through the contemplation that realizes the principle (*tattva*), one attains the four types of knowledge (*jñāna*).
The first consists solely of the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna).
This means that during the stage of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), one falsely conceptualized a real self;
now, having entered the path of seeing (darśanamārga), the notion of a real self is eliminated, and there remains only the phenomena (dharma).
Second, it is not the knowledge of abandonment;
third, it is not the knowledge of one in training (śaikṣa).
This refers to the false conceptualization of annihilationism or eternalism during the stage of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana).
Now, upon entering the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga), one is free from the conceptualization of annihilationism and eternalism;
thus, this is neither the wisdom of annihilation nor the wisdom of permanence.
This is based on the view of annihilation as a conceptual construction (vikalpa), and does not concern the view of annihilation as abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā).
The wisdom that perceives dependent origination as being like an illusory phenomenon refers to the fact that,
whereas during the stage of an ordinary person one falsely gives rise to wrong views, the grasping of views, and the grasping of precepts and rituals,
one now, having entered the path of seeing, skillfully investigates and thus contemplates all phenomena.
This is due to its being like a magical illusion;
it does not exist in the manner conceived by those three types of views and so forth.
This is the first characteristic.
Second, when intense fetters arise due to the loss of mindfulness regarding objects,
he dispels them through mental attention.
Third, he never falls into the miserable realms.
Furthermore, because they have attained the path of remedy even within the miserable realms;
fourth, they do not intentionally violate the precepts;
and fifth, they do not regress or abandon what has been studied.
Jingyun: Because the seeds of delusion have already been severed,
there is no regression or abandonment of the fruits of training.
The Master [Sthiramati] says:
Because one has attained definitive wisdom,
one will certainly not regress from or abandon that which is to be studied.
Sixth, one does not commit the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya-karma*).
Seventh, one definitively knows that suffering and pleasure are not created by oneself and so forth. Jing said:
One knows with certainty that pleasure is not created by a self,

Some become those who will be reborn seven times at most (saptakṛtparama), while others become once-returners (sakṛdāgāmin).
In an age without a Buddha, relying on the body of these two fruits, they do not attain the state of non-returner (anāgāmin) but instead directly realize arhatship.
These latter two types of persons both belong to the class of "group-practitioners" (vargacārin).
At the very least, it does not decrease below four lifetimes;
at the most, it does not exceed one hundred kalpas,
because it does not reach the level of the first person.

The intent of this second section is to clarify three types of pratyekabuddhas: first, those who initially resolve their minds and cultivate the foundation of the path of skillful means; second, those who encounter a Buddha at the time of their initial resolution; and third, those who have already achieved the fruit after practicing for a hundred kalpas, like the rhinoceros-horn type.

Now, the treatise explains this separately: after having already encountered the era of a Buddha during one hundred kalpas, furthermore, although one has practiced within those hundred kalpas, one has not yet cultivated skillfulness regarding the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth;
only after passing through these hundred kalpas and encountering the era of a Buddha does one then cultivate skillfulness regarding the aggregates.
In their final body, they attain the path of the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddha].
Regarding the second type of path, they first encounter a Buddha who preaches the Dharma for them;
they do not require more than one hundred kalpas of cultivation.
Having practiced for either ninety kalpas or even down to one kalpa,
they cultivate skill in the aggregates and so forth within the stages of "Heat" (ūṣmagata) and the others.
In this body, one cannot realize the ultimate fruit;
rather, one may realize the first fruit, or become a *kulaṃkula*, a *saptakṛtvaḥparama*, a *sakṛdāgāmin*, or an *antarāparinirvāyin*, and so forth,
attaining the fruit of a *pratyekabuddha* in a subsequent body.
Having encountered a Buddha on the third path and practiced there, they attain the first fruit (*srotāpatti*) in this very body;
or else they attain the fruits of one born seven times at most (*saptakṛtvah-parama*), a family-to-family practitioner (*kulaṃkula*), a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), or a non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
Subsequently, by cultivating skillfulness regarding the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, they realize the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha Arhat in a future life.
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 26, there are two meanings for "Pratyekabuddha":
first, the Solitary Realizer (*Pratyekabuddha*);
second, the One Awakened through Conditions (*Nidānabuddha*).
As for the Pratyekabuddha described above,
such a person attains the Way in this present life;
they awaken by themselves without hearing it from another.
These are called Pratyekabuddhas.
There are two kinds of Pratyekabuddhas:
one kind was originally an enlightened person.
He was born among those who were still training,
at a time when no Buddha existed and the Buddha-dharma had ceased.
This srotāpanna has already completed seven births;
he shall not undergo an eighth birth,
as he will personally attain the realization of the Way.
Such a person is not called a Buddha nor is he called an Arhat; he is called a minor Pratyekabuddha.
He is no different from an Arhat, though there may be some who are not equal to great Arhats such as Śāriputra.
A great pratyekabuddha, having cultivated merit and increased wisdom throughout one hundred kalpas,
attains a portion of the thirty-two marks;
there may be thirty-one marks.
Whether possessing thirty, twenty-nine, or even down to a single mark among the nine types of arhats, their wisdom is sharp and superior;
regarding all profound dharmas, they [discern] both general and specific characteristics.
One who is able to enter long-cultivated meditative concentration and constantly delights in solitary dwelling with such characteristics is called a Mahāpratyekabuddha.
Furthermore, if one follows the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, it is taught as the superior explanation that there is a single practice for a single fruit.
Regarding the "practice" (*xi*),
the Tripiṭaka Master said:
The second person previously possessed both the qualities of a śrāvaka and a pratyekabuddha; thus,
having cultivated the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) as a śrāvaka,
he encountered another Buddha during three further lifetimes.
By changing one's faculties, one attains the lineage of a pratyekabuddha,
enabling the wholesome roots of the *nirvedhabhāgīya* conducive to pratyekabuddhahood to arise in the present.
As for the third person:
The first three fruits [of the path], having encountered the appearance of a Buddha in the world, are transformed into Pratyekabuddhas;
they are not ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana).
Therefore, the fruit of Non-returner (anāgāmin) is called the ultimate point.
Jingyun’s path of skillful means was accomplished;
he further cultivated the practice of entering the contemplation of the truths and the cultivation of the three characteristics,
as has already been explained in the preceding section.

It is known that those who have attained the third fruit as solitary realizers (pratyekabuddhas), having entered the state of sainthood, are unable to fulfill it completely and must undergo further rebirths;
these belong to the first two fruits and are not non-returners (anāgāmin).
If they are of the non-retrogressive type, they cannot exhaust all outflows while remaining in that fruit.
Upon the end of their lives, they are reborn in the higher realms.

Since there are no Pratyekabuddhas who are reborn in the higher realms, we know that the third type of Pratyekabuddha encounters a Buddha, generates the aspiration for enlightenment, practices the path, and enters the state of an Arya.
Those who pass away without having exhausted all outflows are those in the first two fruits;
this is determined by the subsequent text itself.
The first is called the rhinoceros-horn [pratyekabuddha];
the latter two are called the group-dwelling [pratyekabuddhas].
Master Ji says that there are three types of practice.
The first is as stated in the text.
The second consists of two types because the aforementioned path has two;
therefore, cultivation (*abhyāsa*) likewise has two types.
The explanation of "abiding" (vihāra) follows the text.
Within the section on "conduct" (caryā), all aspects are collectively raised to clarify their characteristics.

It states that one merely manifests supernatural powers (ṛddhi) without preaching the Dharma, and so forth, until reaching the point where one has from the beginning been exclusively inclined toward tranquility (śama). Jing says: "This relies on the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (or *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*), Chapter Thirteen."
A person belonging to the vehicle of the solitary realizers (pratyekabuddha-yāna) is one who possesses the nature of a solitary realizer;
whether their [attainment] is certain or uncertain, they are of middling faculties.
Seeking liberation for oneself,
one generates vast and correct aspirations and cultivates the intention of renunciation and detachment from craving for the sake of liberation.
Furthermore, cultivating the aspiration for the realization of solitary enlightenment,
one takes the Śrāvaka Piṭaka as the object of focus and diligently practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma (dharmānudharmapratipatti).
Either they have not yet previously arisen the aids to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya), or they have already previously arisen them;
or they have not yet previously attained the fruits [of the path], or they have already previously attained them.
In an age without a Buddha, one may dwell as a rhinoceros-like pratyekabuddha through internal reflection alone until the Noble Path manifests before them; or,
as one of the solitary or group-dwelling pratyekabuddhas, one attains the end of suffering.

If one has not previously arisen in the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) nor attained the fruits [of the path], only then does one become a rhinoceros-like solitary dweller (*khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa-pratyekabuddha*).
As for the rest who practice as members of the superior group of solitary realizers (*vargacārin*), [the case is otherwise].
This meaning is largely consistent with the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
Alternatively, those who have not yet produced the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are the first type of person in the *yoga*;
those who have already produced the aids to penetration correspond to the latter two types of persons in the *yoga*.
Alternatively, those who have not yet attained the fruit prior to yoga correspond to the first two types of practitioners;
those who have already attained the fruit prior to yoga correspond to the third type of practitioner.
The first type becomes a rhinoceros-like [solitary buddha].
The latter two constitute the group-practice (gaṇacaryā),
which is likewise identical to the Yoga [Tantras].
As for the statement "whether fixed or unfixed":

The first type of person cultivates the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) during a hundred kalpas, and only in their final body do they give rise to the stages of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, whereby they immediately exhaust all outflows; this differs from the Śrāvakas and is termed "definite.

The second and third types encounter a Buddha and resolve their minds [on enlightenment]; they may either merely give rise to the stages of "Heat" and so forth, or they may also enter the noble state and realize the fruit of Stream-entry (*srotāpanna*); being similar to the Śrāvakas, these are termed "indefinite."
Furthermore, within the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas, if one matures only the lineage of a Pratyekabuddha, this is termed "fixed";
if one matures the lineages of other vehicles as well, this is termed "unfixed."

The explanation in this text is the same as that in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, which mentions only those established in meditative concentration (*samāpatti*) while omitting a detailed distinction for those not so established—namely, the Pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma* states: "Just as it is said that there are two types of Stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*)."
First, gradual deliverance is as previously described.

Second, instantaneous deliverance refers to having entered the clear realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*) and, relying on the *anāgamya* concentration, giving rise to a supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*) that instantaneously abandons all afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms.
Each category is abandoned separately;
only two fruits are established, namely the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of arhatship.
By means of these two fruits, one permanently abandons, respectively, the afflictions of the three realms that are to be abandoned through seeing and those to be abandoned through cultivation.
Because they are manifested by the state of having nothing remaining (*anupadhiśeṣa*), the two intermediate fruits are not established;

for it is only through the abandonment of the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that these states are manifested as "with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*) and "without remainder. Furthermore, with reference to such a person who attains liberation all at once (*sakṛnnairyāṇika*), the Sūtra states that immediately after the stage of stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), one is established as an arhat.
Such a person, either in the present life or at the time of death, will skillfully discern the noble intent.
Even if they cannot accomplish it then, by the power of their aspiration, they will be reborn in the desire realm during a world devoid of a Buddha and achieve the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha.
The latter portion of the text states: "If one is unable to accomplish it because one has not yet been able to leave all desires without remainder,
and thus takes birth in the desire realm through the power of aspiration,
that person will be able to swiftly realize parinirvāṇa."
It is said that those of an indeterminate nature among the śrāvakas,
having attained the stage of stream-entry (srotāpanna), desire to transcend it and attain arhatship but are unable to do so;
by the power of their vows, they emerge in a world devoid of a Buddha and achieve the fruit of a pratyekabuddha.
By virtue of this vow, he turns his aspiration toward pratyekabuddhahood and immediately abides in the first fruit;
or, after seven births, in his final body, he exhausts the remaining fetters and realizes pratyekabuddhahood.
These are what are called Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
As for the statement that "all from the beginning have always been inclined toward tranquility," they are called "inclined toward tranquility" because their nature delights in stillness.
It is not meant that all are of a definitive nature destined for tranquility (*śama*).
